speechtext: House resumed adjourned debate on the motion of Sir Wilfrid Laurier for the House to go into committee on a certain proposed resolution respecting the construction of a National Transcontinental Railway.

When the debate adjourned last evening, Mr. Speaker, I was speaking of the benefits which will result to the country, in the way of colonization, from the scheme now under discussion. I was pointing out that the lands along the route of the proposed railway would he very much more enhanced in value, and I propose to dwell for a moment on this point of the question more particularly as regards that portion of the route with which I am familiar. I know that in the province of New Brunswick the sections which will be opened up by this railway are very rich in agricultural and other resources and only require greater railway facilities to become centres of settlement. In those districts there are rich forest preserves, which have as yet scarcely been touched. Only those portions near the streams have been worked, leaving vast regions from which immense stores of wealth can be taken. There are besides abundant mineral resources and a soil well adapted for agriculture. In the constituency represented by my bon. friend from Queen's and Sunbury (Mr. Wilmot) there are rich coal deposits, which only need to be brought into touch with the market. So that from whatever point of view you choose to look at it, the projected line through that province cannot fail to promote settlement, to enhance the value of land, and aid in the development of rich forest and mineral resources. Coming to the province of Quebec, with which I am of course not quite so familiar, I have been fortunate enough to have had placed in my hands a reference, which I think will prove that the portion of that province to be opened up by tbis transcontinental railway is a very promising one. For many years there has been a strong desire on tlie part of people living in that section, who are familiar with its fertility and resources, for railway facilities. In 1884, the then member for Bellechasse in the

Quebec legislature, tlie late Fauclier de St. Maurice, who was one of the leaders of the Conservative party of that day, and far more patriotic' than any possessed by that party to-day, read in the Assembly a letter from the Reverend Mr. G. Boulet, parish priest of St. Magloire, in which that clergyman said :-
I see by the press that you and your friends are working to have a railway built which will pass along the southern front of the county of Dorchester, Bellechasse, Montmagny, L'Islet and Kamouraska. That would be a grand and patriotic undertaking, a most happy conception, one that should long since have been realized.
That is exactly the line to be taken by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway except that it crosses the county at Levis instead of Dorchester.
In rear of the above named counties there is a magnificent valley, most suitable for the construction of a railway. It is neither hilly nor rocky. Starting from Metgermette, sloping down to Edmundston, there is a regular and fertile plain. Any company that would undertake to build a railway there would find all the necessary material on the ground. Cedar and spruce abound.
Well, Sir, Edmundston and the valley that extends to it in New Brunswick, is exactly the land over which the new line is proposed to be built.
Why do not our governments direct their colonizing and improving energies in that direction. The soil is suited to all kinds of cultivation, the climate is milder than the northern one of the Saguenay region.
This is exactly what my right lion, friend the Prime Minister proposes doing, but which the Conservative party of to-dayunworthy descendants of men like Fauclier -will have none of. It was Mr. Fauclier de Saint Maurice who said :
From the south shore of the St. Lawrence is the frontier of Maine, the land must be rescued from its unvisited isolation, and that heart of New Brunswick must be opened, but by an artery that will send its pulsations east and west to give life to the commerce of our country. But it is the federal, not the provincial government that must accomplish the work.
Further on he said :
Unfortunately my influence, humble as it is. goes not beyond the provincial sphere, but some day, men of large views and iron nerves will arise to accomplish the patriotic task, which the letter I have read so recommends, and whomsoever they may be, future generations will bless them.
These were the utterances in 1884 of one of the Conservative leaders of that day, and an eminent litterateur, in whose footprints the Tartes, the Casgrains, the Monks and others of our day were ever proud to follow. This shows the opinion held at that period of the rich resources of that section of the province of Quebec, which hon. gentlemen opposite are now so anxious to decry. From Moncton to the in-Mr. EMMERSON.
terior of New Brunswick, through the counties of Queen's, York, Carleton, Victoria, Madawaska, on into the province of Quebec, there is a long unbroken line of country, rich in agricultural mineral and forest wealth.
I do not look upon this scheme as merely one for the purpose of finding an outlet for the rich products of the west. If It were necessary, it would be well perhaps to have it for that alone. But when you combine the other attractive feature, the development of the country, with that of colonization, it certainly is a scheme which must commend itself to the people of our day in Canada. It certainly will receive the plaudits of those who are to come after us, of those who will enjoy the rich benefits which, will result from the accomplishment of this great project.
Now we are told that in northern Quebec there are conditions very similar in character to the conditions which exist in that section to which I have just now referred. There always has been, and is to-day, I believe, a great desire in tlie province of Quebec to colonize its undeveloped country. Away back in 1853, and from that time down, the cry through that province has been, Colonize. The national poet of French Canada gave the watchword to the people when he said, ' Let us take possession of tlie soil.' He wanted them to enter the forest, to open up roads, to establish settlements, and to turn a desert region into gardens of plenty. For fifty years the people have been called upon to push forward colonization projects, but they could not respond to the call. It was easier for their young men, as it was easier for the young men of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, to cross over into the borderland, to go into the great neighbouring republic, and as a result tlie New England States contain today, I might almost say, millions of the bone and sinew, of the brawn and brain of our maritime provinces and of the province of Quebec. This is more true of those provinces than it is of the province of Ontario, because in Ontario the people have enjoyed the developing influences of railways. * It is true, they have made many sacrifices to obtain these railways, they have adopted schemes of bonusing railways by the municipalities, and they have had great assistance from their national and provincial governments. But even there the blighting influence of these enticing calls from tlie southern republic has been felt, and this is further true in the maritime provinces and tlie province of Quebec. If these young men could have been kept in our country, they would have helped to build up Canada, they would have found means of earning their way into tlie vast regions of our northern country. This railway now contemplated will do all this for our young men who are now living here ; it will do more, it will invite people from abroad. It will estab-

lisli settlements, It will broaden ont our settled area, and it will increase tlie value of our great domain. This railway will create a highway through the heart of a region which possesses untold resources, the wealth of which, for petty political reasons, the opposition of to-day are willing to deny. They are ready and willing to hold their country up to the wide world as a land confined to a few valleys, the greater portion of which is as barren as the Tartar steppes. I was pained to hear my hon. friend the ex-Miu-ister of Railways refer to his province of New Brunswick in the way he did. lie was willing to hold up that province as one the greater portion of which did not contain resources worthy of consideration. It seems to me lie has not, in that respect, done justice to his own province.
Speaking in a general way, the line from Quebec westward will pass along the northern slope, as I understand it, of the Lam-entinns, and that dividing line will cut through the vast valleys out of which spring the Batiscan, the St. Maurice, the Gatineau, the Coulonge, the Desmoines, and the Ottawa rivers. From the best sources of information that is from men who have travelled over and over again through these great sections, the resources of that country are three-fold-forest, mineral and agricultural. On the Batiscan, away north beyond the parish of St. Narcisse, there fj'fe forests of spruce which extend westward and northward all along that line, in addition to the pine and spruce forests north of the rivers I have just mentioned.
May I interrupt the hon. gentleman to ask what report he is reading from ?
I am not reading from a report.
I thought he was reading from some clergyman's report.
My hon. friend will pardon me, I am only giving him some information which I am sure will be of benefit to him, because it relates to the province of Quebec.
I am delighted, Mr. Speaker, to hear his remarks, but 1 thought he was reading from some clergyman's report.
Well, it would certainly' be much better if it were from a clergyman's report.
The hon. gentleman would appreciate it all the more.

My hon. friend, I know, likes things tinged with theology ; perhaps he would appreciate still more anything that was tinged with religion, but in this case I am not drawing for him a religious picture. The proposed line will run through a region of country that will supply the pulp industries of the world for a century to come.
The reports which have been read to this House, containing the information which I am endeavouring to give at this moment, are confirmatory of all that has been said in regard to it in official documents. The province of Quebec have sent out many exploring parties into that section of the country, and in the archives of the province are records showing the great value of the resources of that region, giving full information as to its topography and as to its mineral, agricultural and forest wealth. We cannot shut our eyes to these facts. It is all very well to say there is no information; it is all very well to refuse to accept the information which comes to us from all these sources. In the days when the Canadian Pacific Railway was projected we did not have any such information with regard to that proposed line as we have to-day with respect to the projected line now under discussion.
I think one hon. gentleman stated in the House that in all that region you could not find a tree as large as a man's leg. That is an assertion tending, as I think, to mislead the country. And it is easy to make such assertions. It is easy to deal in a spirit of levity even with important matters like this ; but that spirit should not characterize the utterances of hon. members of this House, especially when dealing with a project of this character. For this is not a question merely of and. for to-day. This is a work for the future of our country, and it is one that is fraught with great possi-'bilities, not merely for us, but for our children, and not merely for us and for our children, but for those who shall come into this country. We are putting forth our best efforts day by day and year by year to influence the best citizenship of other countries to come to our land, where they can build for themselves homes under conditions that offer them every hope of prosperity and happiness. Now, as I understand, there is in the Crown Lands Department of Quebec, information of an official character which refutes the insinuation covered by remarks such as the one to which I have just referred. And, while it may be asserted in this House for a purpose, that that country has no rich timber resources and offers no opportunity for industry, we know that the statement is refuted by the actual conditions prevailing in the province of Quebec. Annually the government there have their sales of timber limits ; and what values are placed by the business men engaged in the great lumber and pulp industry upon the privileges offer: ed at these sales ? We know that the highest prices are obtained by the Quebec government for these timber limits. Business men, looking for investment for their capital, attach greater value to the resources of that country than hon. gentlemen opposite seem to do. The fact that these men place so high a value upon the timber resources

of that region Would alone justify tlie government in deciding that this land must have railway facilities, apart altogether from the grander scheme of furnishing ' spout,' as it is called, for the great grain reservoir of the west through Canadian territory to Canadian seaports. The government should not lose sight, and I am sure does not lose sight of the importance of settling and peopling that timber region, and developing and working the resources of sections which are now, in a sense, isolated and removed from civilizing influence of railways and centres of population. It is objected that these timbered lands are watered by rivers which flow towards the markets of the country, and that they afford channels by which the timber can be more readily and cheaply brought to market than can be done by railway. That may be true of certain strips of land bordering these rivers. But we all know that there are heights beyond, that there are sections somewhat remote from these rivers which the lumberman cannot tap, so that their rich timber resources lie dormant. We know that that country has these great timber resources, or whence come the vast quantities of pine that float down the Gatineau, the Colounge, the Des-inoines and Black rivers ? For a hundred miles beyond	the timber	limits now	leasedand worked,	there	are	pine and	spruceforests, as I am informed, but they cannot be worked, because there are no railway facilities, and because, as they lie north of the height of	land,	the	rivers flow	northward, and so	carry	the	timber away from
and not to the market. As I understand it, this railway will be on the northern side of the Laurentian range, and it will be to the northern side what the rivers I have named are to the forest wealth of this side of the slope. I am also informed that there are rich mineral deposits, particularly of phosphate, as well as deposits of precious ores. This is, perhaps, in a sense, conjecture. The value of an undeveloped mineral country is, after all, a matter of conjecture and speculation ; until you have your mines actually working, even the fairest prospect cannot be counted upon as a certainty. The geological formation of the Laurentian does not change as you go north ; it is the same great upheaval, and the same conditions prevail. What is to De found in its strata on this side of the range is to be found on the other side also, but in what proportion remains to be discovered. All this will be discovered when this railway shall have made if worth while for the prospector and the miner to undergo the toil and incur the expense necessary. The road, as designed, will pass along a chain of lafies that extends, link by link, from Lake St. John, in the east, to Lake Abbittibi, in the west. That the Lake St. John country is an agricultural region no one can deny. Only those who know nothing about will venture to deny it.
The land is exactly of the same character as the land to the westward. The soil is watered by a similar source, and enjoys similar conditions conducive to fertility.
Is this road supposed to go from Quebec to Lake St. John ?
No.
Then why is Lake St. John- included in the description of the route of this road ?

It does not go to Lake St. John. There is a road now to Lake St. John. This road goes from Quebec. 1 refer to Lake St. John as the eastern extremity of a region which is rich as an agricultural section, and I say that there are continuous links of lakes running eastward from Lake St. John, that the Lake St. John region is known to be rich and that the country surrounding the other lakes to the westward is of the same character.
You are all wrong.

My hon. friend from Torouto (Mr. Brock) shakes his head. Anybody who knows nothing about it is in a position to deny, but those who understand it, those who have information upon the subject, are not in that position. There is one thing that is known and known to a verity, and that is that there are very many rich farms to the north of us on the Gatineau river, along the Desert, and on the Baska-tonge. Even to-day, without these facilities, the pioneer has gone in and he has demonstrated that there can be carved out in that region rich and flourishing sections of agricultural country. I am informed that only the other day there left the city- of Montreal a colonizing expedition to visit this rich, this fertile, this splendid section of country, and I fancy that the very anticipation of this line of railway is what has induced these adventurers to go into that section of the country. They want to pre-empt the land for future occupation, they have gone there for that purpose, and already the fruits of this scheme are becoming evident in the province of Quebec. There are away north in sections of the country not penetrated by others than the explorer fine farms that have been snatched from the wilderness by the lumber operators. These farms are well situated, only that they require facilities for marketing. They are situated on the shores of lakes or streams or on the slopes of the hillsides. All this is evidence of the fact that there are in the provinces of Quebec and New Brunswick-I shall not refer to the province of Ontario as we are all familiar with what has been said in respect to that province-lying alongside the proposed route of this road lands rich in forest wealth and having prospects of rich mineral resources. These require development, and in their development settlements will be established and new constituencies created. In the province of

New Brunswick we are complaining and suffering to-day from the fact that we are losing at this redistribution a seat in this House. In the province of Ontario, they are losing, 1 think, six representatives, and if it had not been for the results of the Canadian Pacific Railway in the Algoma district, Ontario would have lost more than six. Now, these provinces, in order to retain their representation, must have the development of those sections of country which are now lying dead and dormant. The hope of New Brunswick lies now upon its great interior, in the development of its mineral resources, in making marketable its rich forest wealth and in the creation of rich agricultural districts. Decade after decade they are losing their representatives on the floor of this House. There must be something done to arrest this decay, and the same is true in respect of Ontario. If the Canadian Pacific Railway could establish settlements and assemble population to the extent of thousands and tens of thousands in the Algoma district to the north of the Nipissing, surely these other provinces by reason of this scheme, this railway, being projected through them can establish settlements, can make additions to the population, and effect the maintenance of the status of the provinces in the Dominion. Now, Mr. Speaker, I am sure that where so much has been said on this subject I will be only wearying the House and worrying myself if I were to attempt to elaborate more on this subject. It is fruitful of discussion, and I am sure, in a sense, very profitable, but there are other features of this scheme with which I desire to deal, and they are practically the features which while it is not sectional, will affect in a marked degree the constituency from which I come. I have said that the leadership in the criticism and condemnation of the Bill now under discussion comes from a gentleman who has for many years been the leader from New Brunswick in the councils of the executive of this Dominion. A gentleman who has held a very high position not only in his own province, but in the cabinet of the Dominion, and who has wielded a very marked influence, and I am bound to say worthily wielded that influence. The very fact that he criticises and condemns this measure, as hon. members know, must necessarily have an influence.
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend (Mr. Brock) says ' hear, hear,' and quite true. It would be very strange if it were not so and yet I think it is due to the members of this House that they should inquire into the character of that criticism and condemnation. The fact that he has criticised and condemned the measure caused a great up-heavel amongst gentlemen opposite. I could see a glow in their countenances.
At the conclusion of the speech these hon. gentlemen so delighted with the utterances of the ex-minister, were forgetful of the past. I could not hear an echo of anything that had occurred with respect to that hon. gentleman in the very recent past, nor could I see any evidence of memory on their part, as to what they had been saying about him for the past seven or ten years. I realize that when men die nothing but good is said of them, and that in many instances they are sainted. When a Liberal departs from the ranks of his party and gives comfort to our opponents, these gentlemen canonize him, and we hear from them not a hint of Drummond steals or of Tarte traitors. That is all forgotten, and these gentlemen cherish the idea that there can be wiped out from memory for all time, that which they have done and said. It was amusing to see our Conservative friends cross the floor of the House at the conclusion of that speech and congratulate the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals. Their leader headed the phalanx and one after another they crossed the floor to felicitate their former opponent.	_
It is my purpose to consider and to discuss the utterances of that hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Blair) particularly in connection with the features of this scheme between Moncton and Quebec. In the first place, the hon. gentleman said that there should not be a railway constructed from Levis to Moncton over the route indicated, because it'would parallel and duplicate the present Intercolonial Railway, and in liis letter to the Premier the hon. gentleman stated that it was practically because of tliat proposal that he resigned his portfolio. In taking that high moral ground, as he claims conscientiously, he has perhaps unconsciously ascribed to himself a monopoly of all the conscience and high moral tone which may appertain to members from the pro\ ince of New Brunswick. He insinuates that those who differ from him are not actuated by the same high moral attributes which lie possesses. Indeed, the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Blair) went so far as to say once in this House, that there was no one in the*province of New Brunswick who favoured the proposed railway between Quebec and Moncton except those who hoped to profit by the expenditure of the money. A more unworthy stigma was never cast upon the people of New Brunswick, and coming from so high an authority it is worth inquiring how far it may be true. The hon. gentleman admitted that the city council of Moncton passed a resolution favouring the scheme, but he said in effect, that they would not have passed that resolution if they only waited to learn all about it from liini. Let us remember that the Moncton city council is constituted without logaid to ' federal political lines, that there are Liberals and Conservatives in that council and that the mayor of the city is a Conser-

vative. That council unanimously passed a resolution favouring this scheme in its entirety, and favouring it unequivocally and without reservation. Later on, the Moncton Board of Trade discussed the matter as they had discussed it six or eight months before, at which time they favoured by resolution practically the scheme which has been adopted. In their recent resolution the board of trade declared strongly in favour of the scheme, but not unanimously. There were actually two who opposed the resolution. One of them, I believe, is the managing director or president of the board of directors of the ' Times ' Publishing Company, a newspaper which neither at the present time nor in the past has supported anything that savoured of Liberalism The other opponent of that resolution was the editor of that newspaper. These two were against the leading Conservative business men, and against the leading Liberal business men, and against the citizens of Moncton generally. These two gentlemen stand on record, the lonely two in the city of Moncton, opposed to the construction of that line between Moncton and Quebec. However, they do not count, and therefore it may very well be said that the Moncton Board of Trade is unanimous in favour of the government scheme.
The first objection made by the ex-minister (Hon. Mr. Blair) to that line, is that it parallels and duplicates the Intercolonial Kailway. It seems to me, however, that it is possible that two lines of railway may connect at the same points, and at the same time one need not necessarily be a paralleling or a duplicating of the other. It is a new idea that because two points are connected by a certain railway there shall consequently be no other railway built to connect these same points. Why, Sir, the records of parliament are teeming with illustrations antagonistic of that principle. For years in New Brunswick we have been practically doing the same thing as is now proposed, and the same rule has been applied throughout the Dominion. I am informed that the Department of Railways and Canals administered by the ex-minister in 1899 bonused the Lake Erie and Detroit River Railway to parallel the Michigan Central from Ridgetown to St. Thomas, a distance of 44 miles, and that these two railways only varied in distance from each other, from a few rods at the minimum to about four miles at the maximum. The government gave that bonus on condition that the Lake Erie Company could not secure adequate running rights over the Michigan Central. When the ex-minister stated that the proposed line from Quebec to Moncton would parallel the Intercolonial Railway, I am sure that my hon. friend from Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) was one of those who applauded. And yet, in 1899 when the Lake Erie and Detroit River bonus was under consideration, the hon. member for Mr. EMMERSON.
Bothwell moved to strike out the proviso in the resolution, so that the bonus would be given without any condition being attached. He not only spoke, but I find by reference to ' Hansard ' that he was on his feet thirty times in his efforts to have that proviso struck out. More than that, he divided the House on the question. He claimed that the fact that the railway was ruuinng alongside of another was no reason why the government of Canada should withhold aid if it were serving the interests of the coup-try. I will not take up the time of the House in quoting from the speeches in that connection. One of the reasons he advanced why there should be no conditions, was that the Lake Erie road afforded an outlet to the lake shore townships; and yet hon. gentlemen opposite claim that the railway now under consideration, going eastward in the same direction as the Intercolonial, should not be aided by the government of Canada, even though it affords an outlet for the rich and unlimited products of our western country. Then, the Canadian Pacific Railway line was chartered from Toronto to Windsor, although from London to Windsor it runs less than two miles from the Grand Trunk Railway, and for a considerable portion of the way these two railways run side by side like a double track. That principle has been established throughout the Dominion time and time again; it has been established in this parliament; and yet this objection is brought forward as something that should constrain the parliament of Canada to prevent the construction of an all-Canadian railway to Canadian seaports. In the case to which I have referred, my hon. friend from Bothwell urged the repeal of the condition upon which the subsidy was granted, even though the two railways ran practically between the same fences, whereas in the case before us there is beginning a short distance from Levis a range of hills separating the two railways entirely. The Intercolonial serves a very good purpose on the northern slope of these hills, and the proposed railway will serve a like good purpose in furnishing facilities to the residents of the country on their southern slope.
I have referred to the paralleling of the Intercolonial Railway by the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway. The hon ex-Mlnister of Railways and Canals, speaking of paralleling, claims that this railway will dismantle the Intercolonial Railway, and the words are repeated by the hon. member for South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart). While the hon. gentleman wishes to take very high moral ground in reference to this question, he does not refrain from indulging in a line of argument which I consider is a very great descent from the high moral altitude which lie had assumed. He has referred to the construction of the proposed railway as a dismantling of the Intercolonial Railway, and he has claimed that it will not only

injure the traffic of the road, but will simply depopulate the city of Moncton, where the workshops of the Intercolonial Railway are situated. It is all very well to offer an argument of that kind, but it must be based upon such facts as will support it. The hon. member, in the days when he was Minister of Railways and Canals, did not refuse to bonus a railway running from the town of Campbellton, N.B., crossing through the province, and connecting at the St. John river with the Bangor and Aroostook. The railway to which I refer is known as the Restigouche and Western. It commences at Campbellton and runs up the waters of the Restigouche to Matapedia ; thence up the Restigouche to the Upsal-quiteli, thence westerly to the waters of the Tobique river, which it crosses; thence to St. John river at or near Edmundston ; on the other side of the river it connects with what is known as the Bangor and Aroostook Railway system, which communicates with the city of Bangor, in the state of Maine, and thence with the city of Boston by the Maine Central. If the aiding of railways in New Brunswick would injure the Intercolonial Railway, there never was aid given to a railway that would do more damage to the Intercolonial Railway than that one. Because, what was the object of that railway ? It was in order that the people living at Campbellton and along the shores of the Baie des Chaleurs down to the Gasp6 coast should be brought nearer to the American market. They send their fish, their lumber and all their other products to the American market. They seek such a market over the Intercolonial by way of Levis and across through Vermont. This line when completed will afford them railway facilities direct through New Brunswick and through to the state of Maine to the cities on the American seaboard. And yet there was no cry against that railway on the ground of injury to the Intercolonial. The necessities of trade and the interests of the people, it was deemed, demanded its construction, and no cry of that kind was raised. But because to-day, from a national standpoint, it is deemed necessary to have a trunk line of railway from the east to the west, forsooth the Intercolonial must stand as a barrier against it, even though the Intercolonial may not be in a position in any way to carry out the objects designed by the project under discussion.
In this connection, I might say that the lion. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals, when he made the statement as to this road dismantling the Intercolonial, neglected to explain to this House that a few years ago he, as Minister of Railways and Canals? entered into a contract with the Grand Trunk Railway Company whereby that company, for a period of ninety-nine years, or during the existence of that contract, should hand over to the Intercolonial Railway the freight which they gathered in the western
country which is tapped by the Grand Trunk. This freight was to be handed over at Ste. Rosalie or at Montreal, and he failed to inform the House that although the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway may be projected into the maritime provinces, although the section between Quebec and Moncton may be completed and in operation, yet that traffic thus covenanted to be given over to the Intercolonial Railway by the Grand Trunk Railway at Ste. Rosalie and at Montreal must continue to be given to it during ninety-nine years or during the continuance of that agreement. Then will the establishment of this line take away one jot or title of the freight which the Intercolonial Railway receives from the west to-day V By no means. Did he tell the House that the traffic, which is to be carried by the proposed line of railway between Moncton and Winnipeg, is a traffic which is not yet in existence ? Did he say that the Intercolonial Railway receives to-day or has ever received any portion of the traffic from the extreme west ? He knows that the Intercolonial Railway has never received such traffic. He knows that although we have spent millions in the extension of the line from L6vis to Montreal, it was not designed to get traffic from Manitoba and the Territories but to get the Ontario traffic. The object was to get the Intercolonial Railway into the metropolitan city of Canada,' to gather there all the freight possible from the province of Ontario and carry it over the Intercolonial Railway. It was a very wise scheme which time has justified. But this project will in no way interfere with that traffic.	Supposing this line were built
from Winnipeg to Quebec and stopped there, do you think that the Intercolonial Railway would ever receive any portion of the traffic brought from Winnipeg to Quebec ? Only one who. is insane would think so for a moment. We'know that it would not. But what we do know is that the construction of this new line from Quebec to Moncton will add to the prospects of the Intercolonial Railway getting a portion of that traffic. From the city of Moncton to Halifax and St. John, there must be necessarily an increase of traffic by reason of the construction of a short line to Moncton. When the traffic has been brought to Moncton, it must go thence either to St. John or Halifax; and the strong probabilities are that it will necessitate the construction of another track between Moncton and Halifax. Nor did the hon. gentleman say anything with respect to the traffic that may come from the west, and which can continue over the Intercolonial Railway as far as Truro and then down to Sydney. All this shows that the hon. gentleman was endeavouring to excite the animosities, prejudices and passions of the people of Moncton. The people of that city have pronounced unanimously in favour of the project before us; and as a representative of the county of

Westmoreland and having some knowledge of the neighbouring counties, I say that the people are to a man almost unanimously in favour of the construction of this line. They realize what benefits will come from it. They realize that Canada requires to-day a transcontinental line truly Canadian, and they know that the only way to have that is by carrying out to its full fruition the project under discussion.
There is another feature which the hou. gentleman held up as a menace. The shops at Moncton, he predicted, are to be demolished. Well, Sir, the shops of Moncton were there almost to the same extent as they are to-day before the Intercolonial Itail-wav was extended from Levis to Montreal. And engines are now being built at the machine shops connected with the Intercolonial Railway at Moncton. The hon. gentleman knows that the necessities of the road will require that to be continued. I say that the development of the north shore is only in its infancy. I do not think that the Intercolonial has ever had a better friend than I, in my humble way, have endeavoured to be. And I would be very sorry indeed, by act, or vote, or word, to do anything that would in any way interfere with the prosperity of the Intercolonial Railway or the people along its line. I recognize that the Intercolonial has done more for Canada than any other agency. It has cemented the eastern and western provinces together as nothing else has been able to do. It will make it possible for the people in the extreme east to exchange their products with the people of the west, to their mutual aa-vantnge. It will not merely bring us the products of the western prairies, but it will take back to the people there the manufactured products of such centres as Sydney, Halifax, St. John and Moncton. Why, I know as a verity that, to-day, in the city of Moncton, there is an industrial establishment which has increased its capitalization from a quarter of a million to a million of dollars. They are already establishing a branch in the city of Montreal and another branch in the city of Winnipeg. And this railway bringing the. city of St. John two hundred miles nearer to the city of Quebec and to the city of Montreal, and bringing the city of Moncton at least one hundred and forty miles nearer to the city of Montreal, will enable this company, as" it will enable others, to carry on their

business to greater advantage. And surely these are considerations which should move us. I am willing, even if we did not gain any local benefit at all, to vote in favour of the people of Canada contributing of their means for the building of a national highway through our own territory to our own ports. I am not voting or speaking in any selfish or local spirit. But I do realize that the advantage to be gained through this road will be mutual ; I realize that the greater facilities for transportation that It will offer to the producer of the west and the manufacturer of the east, will enrich every section of the country and the country as a whole.
There is one thing to which I feel I should make reference, although I do so with some hesitation, because I know, that, in a sense, the matter is treated as merely academic. Those who have paid any attention to the course which I have pursued in relation to this railway project, if any have done me the honour to observe that course, will know that I have advocated, not merely in this House, but in the Railway Committee, the extension of the Intercolonial Railway into the west and the operation of railways by government. The government owning and operating that road could assemble the western traffic, bring it to the city of Quebec, and pass it along over their Intercolonial Railway, even at the longer haul, assuring to our own eastern ports that traffic, even thougli this were done at a loss. I was honest in my conviction, and am very strongly in favour of the ownership and operation of railways by governments. But I found that when I made that suggestion, even before the Railway Committee, it did not meet with any hearty response from any section. I did not find hon. gentlemen opposite very enthusiastic in then-approval of that idea. And I have had sufficient experience in public life to realize quite clearly that, however Strong the view I may entertain, however conscientious, sincere and earnest I may be, my view cannot prevail against the views of the majority. Government is a matter of compromise, and when we could not have that which I advocated, as I stated before that committee when this matter was being discussed, I accepted the next best thing, and I considered that the next best thing was the government construction and ownership of the spout from the wheat fields of the west to the shores of the Canadian Atlantic.
Now, what does that accomplish ? It insures the regulation of rates, it insures a control over the traffic, it makes it possible for the government, while not suffering the disadvantages of government operation, to enjoy the other advantages incident to the government ownership and operation of railways. I realized this when that measure came before the committee. It will be remembered that the proposition was to build a railway from the west to
the city of Quebec, where it was to stop ; arl,l I realized that if that were done the maritime seaports during the winter months would not in any sense participate in the traflic that would be brought through. Why? Because it would be a company-owned road and a company-operated road down to the city of Quebec, which port they would utilize- during the season of navigation, and that at the close of the season they would seek ports more to their advantage, even though those ports were in the United States.

Mr. EMMEItSON. They are tied up already, and there are provisions in the lease which will bind them hand and foot so that they cannot do more than that. We have done more, we have not merely tied them up by reason of what is contained in that contract, but we have made it to their interest to bring this traffic over to the maritime provinces. Now, I discriminate between the Intercolonial being extended at the expense of Canada, and bringing freight down over the Intercolonial to the seaport; I realize the distinction between that and a company-owned road which stopped at Quebec and then attempted to use the Intercolonial with respect to its winter traffic. Realizing that,
I feel that the present arrangement is one that brings to the Canadian people practically all the advantages of government ownership, and it removes from the people the disadvantages which are incident, certainly in the opinion of many members on both sides of this House, to the government operation of railways. Now, this question of government ownership is one of vast importance, and I know how strongly the people in my own section of the country feel in favbur of that idea. I am also conscious of the disadvantages connected with it. I know that while the govern-

meat could own the road and perhaps operate it to the city of Winnipeg, yet when they came to operate a road from Winnipeg westward they would be met with obstacles which are, as they have been presented to us, almost insurmountable. Take the history of the Canadian Pacific Railway. In order to make their railway successful they have been obliged to establish hotels all along the line. Every one who has gone over that line through the Rockies and around the prairies, has found in all the' large cities hotels established and run by the Canadian Pacific Railway corporation. Could a government do that? There is not enough elasticity in government mangemeut to enable a government to do that. It would be necessary also, having reached the extreme west, to establish a line of steamships for the Orient. Would it be possible for the government to engage in operations of that kind? I know the difficulty which has been experienced in government management of the Intercolonial. If a new business were proposed to be established along the line of the Intercolonial, or if it were necessary Jo seek some concessions necessary, creating business for that road, some rates that would be reasonable, some provisions to make connections, the first thing the promoter of that scheme would do would be to come to the general manager and explain it. The general manager would say, I will consult the Minister of Railways and Canals. He would consult the Minister of Railways and Canals, and perhaps after a long period of time, the matter having been forgotten, another interview would be arranged, the promoter, the minister and the manager would meet together, and perhaps they would finally arrange upon some plan. But time would go on, parliament would have to be consulted, the proposals would be made by the minister, opposition would come from hon. gentlemen opposite, who would look with suspicion upon them, who would criticise them and oppose them, with the result that the man, wearied by the delay, would perhaps go over and make an arrangement with the Canadian Pacific Railway. Why, Sir, I know that has been the case in many instances. I remember an occasion when there was a derelict vessel in the port of Halifax not able to carry its cargo to the destination, and application was made-this was some years ago- to the management at Moncton for a rate that would enable them to take that cargo by railway to its destination. The reply came back from Moncton, we will refer to Ottawa. It was referred to Ottawa, and six months afterwards a reply came to the city of Halifax. Is that elasticity ? Does that show that government management of railwavs is of a satisfactory character ? We realize the fact that the Canadian Pacific Railway and other great railway organizations have a corps of specialists going

through the territory through which then-railways run, instructing the farmers in the establishment and operation of creameries and dairies with the object of creating a traffic for these roads, advocating the interests of the railways, it is true, but, incidentally advancing the interests of the country at the same time. They are in this manner building up and advancing the trade of the country. Could the government do that ? Would the government do it ? Strong as I am in favour of government ownership, I recognize the advantages incident to the operations of corporations in that direction. In the province of New Brunswick the gentleman who has been for a period superintendent of the Canadian Pacific Railway, Mr. Oborne-I think he has since been removed-has actually had established a stock farm or depot for the purchase of cattle in order that the railway should have the benefit of transporting these cattle to the ranches of the west, as was indicated by the hon. Minister of the Interior in his speech. That industry is being carried ou to-day by the Canadian Pacific Railway in New Brunswick. I know, as a matter of fact, that when I was connected with the government of New Brunsick. the superintendent of the Canadian Pacific Railway frequently consulted the government in respect to the assistance that should be afforded in the establishment of dairies and creameries, in building up traffic along the line, and in the creation of traffic, and I am glad to say that in some slight measure, at least, the government was then, as it has been since that day, in a position to aid in the upbuilding of that traffic. It is all necessary, and while government ownership has its advantages there are connected with it some disadvantages which we should not lose sight of. However, I have felt that when you cannot get the best thing, or What you think the best thing in the interests of your constituents and in the interests of the country, it is always wise to accept the next best thing, and I am proud that this scheme involves all the elements that it does. I think, while it has been described ns a liy-bred scheme, it is one that combines the advantages of government ownership, escaping its disadvantages, with the advantages of private ownership where private ownership can help to build up the country in a way in which the government could not do, thereby developing the trade of the country, opening up the country colonizing the country and in every way conducing to the advantage of the country. Our country is so great, its resources so varied and exhaustless and there are so many new things to be done, that it makes this problem of public ownership a very difficult one indeed, and if you can combine the advantages of the one with those of the other you have surely measureably gone in the direction of solving the problem. It is not an easy one. The whole question is one of

such eollosal importance that you cannot simply bind yourself hand and foot to a question of government ownership. I wonder how many hon. gentlemen opposite there are who would subscribe to that doctrine. I wonder if the hon. member for South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) would follow the leadership of the hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals in the direction of pubilc ownership. The hon. ex-minister in speaking of this subject, spoke with a vehemence and with a passion in his onslaught on the government which did not characterize his speeches in times past in this parliament when defending the government. Strong advocate though he has been of government ownership, he was yet willing, as shown by the letter he wrote to the right hon. leader of the government, that this scheme should be aided in its entirety to Quebec from the west in the same way that it has been aided on the western sections. As I understand it, although opposed to the scheme as it has been modified, he was willing that there should be a subsidy given in that direction and that the road should be under the control of the Grand Trunk Pacific. He was willing to accept that as an alternative. Surely, as an advocate of government ownership, if he got the measure of government ownership which this scheme provides he should have been willing to have accepted it in its entirety ; with its features of private ownership with government aid by way of a guarantee. I feel that I have perhaps wearied this House in the discussion of this question, which, as X intimated a few moments ago, may be considered an academic) one, but, we must remember that we are making history. We must remember that we are establishing a principle which may be followed in future years and that it is well for us not to lose sight of the main discussion as to whether we have followed a proper and expedient course, because, after all, this question of public ownership is a question of expediency. The scheme which has been agreed upon by the government is one which they deem to be expedient in the interests of the country. In it they combine the two systems. The old system has passed away in its entirety, the new system has been ushered in, and we must understand as to where that new system will lead us. It would be a matter of impossibility for Canada to acquire all the present systems/ of railway, and to operate them. The government could not undertake to conduct their vast operations by direct agency nor could it be expected to extend the service with the rapidity which would be needful. The question perhaps after all may be ranged with that of the speculative as to government ownership, but we have to inquire as to whether we are not having by the proposed scheme many of the advantages if not all the advantages that must be secured to us if Canada were in a position to acquire all 274
the other systems of railways now within its borders, or leaving that alone, leaving that as too colossal a thing to undertake, if Canada were undertaking to make this new road a government road from east to west. There is, not only in the rapid advancement which displays itself on every hand, not only in the methods of industrial production, but in the aims and aspirations of our people, justification for the departure which has already been made and for the policy adopted by the government in this connection.
How much further the trend of events may lead us in this direction, only the future can disclose. But certainly, as representatives of the people we must realize that in going so far we have taken a step in advance, and accomplished some good to the people of Canada. It has been said that private opinions and judicial utterances are at one in concluding that railways are on a plane with the highways of the country. So they are, but only in a sense, because the highway can be used and operated and taken advantage of indiscriminately, whereas, the railway has to be controlled in its operation, and to that extent there is a vast difference between them. At all events, it behooves the people of Canada to consider the matter from the economic point of view, and considered in that light there is only one answer-from an economic standpoint thi's scheme is unrivalled. It gives government aid and support, and yet it does not inflict burdens on the people; in other words, it lends government credit to a government controlled road, although not a government operated road. There are so many objections to government operation of railways, as we saw in the discussion before the committee, that those who hold views in favour of government ownership and coutrol may very well hesitate as to the soundness of these views. The political objections to government operation are very great. I can see at once the weight of these objections, and though they are not easily answered, yet there are answers to them. The danger of party control is not in my judgment so serious after all. It certainly is not sufficiently serious to enable us to decide the question on that consideration alone, and especially when we take into consideration the fact that we must all recognize that large railway corporations have a great political influence. By this scheme of the government we have curbed to a certain extent the political influence that may be exercised by private corporations. Look at the history of the Canadian Pacific Railway. We built the Canadian Pacific Railway, we equipped it, we paid for it, we gave them the money to run it, and they have been running it and making their millions, but the country does not own one cent in it. We all must recognize the influence which that great corporation has wielded: in Canada since 1881. Its influence is felt to-day; its influence I believe is being felt in the discussion of



this question in parliament, and its influence lias been felt since tlie project was first spoken of in the newspapers. Of course, under private ownership there is competition, hut there are also formidable evils. There is the possibility of discrimination in favour of the few as against the many. How many times has this parliament considered the question of discrimination, not merely as between individuals in the matter of tariff rates, but as between communities; as between the long haul and the short haul; as between the carriage of wheat and the carriage of flour; as between the interests of the east as compared with the middle east in connection with freight rates; as between the interests of the west as compared with the middle west; as between local communities and as between those living in the same community ? All these difficulties are incidental to private ownership, and these evils are curbed, controlled, and regulated by this scheme which the government has asked parliament to approve of. The existence of secret and preferential rates on the railways has been such in the past that they have militated against the interests of the country; they have militated against our industrial advancement; they have militated against the industrial advancement of particular communities, and they have created havoc to private enterprise. This scheme which we are now considering, in a measure controls these things, allied as it is with the legislation introduced by the government in the Railway Commission Bill.
Another disadvantage of private ownership lies in the precarious securities which are floated upon the market, and the injury that ensues in financial circles. These securities are ' beared ' and are ' bulled,' and to-day a railway stock may have an apparent value which to-morrow may have dropped to zero. The scheme proposed by the government is such that there cannot be any such fluctuation of values in connection with it. We know the havoc that nas resulted in the United States in connection with speculation in railway stocks. This will be prevented by the government guarantiees because we know that government guarantees have an established value and do not fluctuate between extremes. There is a confidence in them on the part of the people which tends to the preservation of their financial standing. That is something, that ought not to be overlooked in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, at the hour of recess I was referring to the relationship between government ownership and private ownership, and their relative effects upon railway securities. X was showing that by reason of the sudden and extreme changes in the quotations of railway stocks, Mr. EMMERSON.
there was in private ownership danger of a disturbance in financial circles ; and I was pointing out that by the scheme propounded by the government this danger was removed, in as much as the securities placed on the market had a government guarantee, and were therefore more stable and less fluctuating. But this perhaps is a field that should be traversed by the moralist or the economist; and while it may be food for thought for us, it comes more properly within the purview of their inquiry. There is one thing in connection' with government ownership which I am sure is apparent to all, that is, that government service necessarily costs more in proportion than private service. I think hon. members of this House without distinction of party will concede that ; and to that extent it is an argument against public ownership, and certainly against the government operation of railways. Given the same efficiency in management, the same energy and economy-and all this must be assumed-there certainly could not be any objection to the government operation of railways. Another feature of tlie government embarking in a general scheme of ownership of our lines of railway would be the questions that might arise in the future as to the construction of additional lines and of branch lines. There would also be involved, by reason of the pressure that might bo exercised upon parliament, the question of the duplication of railway lines. There might be too tight a rein exercised, or it might be too free. It would all depend on the political pressure that would be brought to bear. To the extent that this might operate either in the one direction or the other, it would be productive of injury to the public interest. You could not be too stinted ; and it would not be in the public interest to have too free a hand. The interest of communities not served by railways, or not having the advantages of government lines, would always be brought to the front and parliament would be besieged time and again for the duplication of lines, in order that these communities might share in the advantages of government-owned railways. All this would be launched into the arena of political warfare. Even the fair adjustment of rates as between different communities, and the rates that could fairly be charged upon the different articles of traffic, would be a football for political parties. That would be a matter of the highest consequence, as there would be depending upon it commanding commercial interests. Of course, we must all look to the future to furnish a more acute condition with respect to railway rates. Such will become more and more controlling, as modern industrial methods are applied and perfected, as business is conducted on a more expansive scale, and with a lessening margin. This feature is not an alarming one, perhaps, and should not be considered as very serious at the

moment, and yet it is one the importance of which should not he minimized. Another argument which is advanced against government ownership, one in which I do not share very largely, is that it restricts the held of private activity, and narrows the scope for individual effort and achievement. A test of the utility of public ownership by the experience of other countries affords nothing convincing either one way or the other. If you take as illustrations the cases of Europe, Australia, or Africa, all of them presenting different conditions, you find nothing to convince you. In the older countries such as Switzerland, Germany and France, the results achieved are certainly not convincing. They are not on the whole against government ownership. Taking the experience of South Africa and the different states in the Australian commonwealth, and of New Zealand, you have nothing that is positive. But, we could not he governed by the results there, even if they were very marked and convincing, as their conditions are entirely different from ours. It makes no difference whether the government is monarchical or democratic ; the results vary with the conditions. In England we recognize the fact of private ownership; but the prevailing geographical conditions have governed the policy pursued by that country. Each railway in Great Britain seems to serve a certain area ; each railway has its own particular sphere of influence ; and the same difficulties are not presented in that country that are to be found in Canada and the United States.
