Moncton and the Intercolonial Railway 588 miles. So, if the route projected is followed, the central route through the province of New Brunswick by way of Chip-man to St. John, you have a saving of distance of at least 200 miles in round numbers, bringing the winter seaport at present used, nearer by that distance to the city of Quebec than it is now by way of the Intercolonial. Surely that is a matter of consideration, a matter of importance, not merely to the citizens of St. John, but to the people of the west and to the people of all Canada in view of the vast traffic that must exist in years to come, indeed a matter of supreme importance, and one that the parliament of Canada should not disregard at this stage. All this shows that the government has been wise in selecting this route and that, even without regard to sectional opinion, without regard to the interest of this or that local community, the aim and object of the government has been to afford facilities in the interest of all Canada. It is claimed that the government should build branch lines from the different points. I say it would not be in the interest of Canada as a whole that this should be done. While personally, as a citizen of New Brunswick, I should like to see such a branch line from Chipman, connecting at Norton for the city of St. John, yet I do not think that that would be a matter of interest to the people of all Canada. If this were done there, it would have to be done at other points. Trade will seek Its appropriate channel, and, according to my idea, the appropriate channel for heavy freight traffic from the west to the Canadian seaboard in winter is the route I have named. The company have taken power and authority to make connection with St. John, and it will inevitably follow that that connection will be made. And it is in the interest of all Canada that she should have it. More than that, it will be in the interest of the Grand Trunk itself, because it will be in their interest to get the best, the closest possible connection and run by the best and shortest route. Now, all this question of route is one which must be determined by the engineers. I recognize the fact that distance is not the only elenient to be taken into consideration. Gradients, curvatures and alignment of the road are of equal importance. They are all of supreme importance in considering the necessities of modern railway transportation. The road must be of a character to allow traffic with the heavy engines and immense trains which are seen on our great systems throughout Canada and the United States. There is another thing which must not be lost sight of, and that is that whatever the railways cost under this scheme, the expenditure will be among the Canadian people and upon Canadian soil. I am sure that will not be lost sight of by the people of Canada when they come to determine upon this question,

when it is submitted to them for their approval.
I fear that I have wearied the House in going over so much and repeating, as I have been obliged to do, a great deal of what has been said before, and very much better said. But 1 would like to emphasize this one point, that if you remove from this discussion the speech of the hon. ex-Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Blair)-and he built up his argument by taking an extreme view and using what I may characterize, without offence, as very extreme and extravagant language-you find that nothing has been said against the bargain that has been made between the government and the Grand Trunk Pacific. I have listened to all the speeches delivered by the gentlemen on the other side, and they have in no sense assailed tiie bargain. They have not punctured it in even one little essential. The bargain is recognized to be in the interest of the people of Canada, and hon. gentlemen opposite cannot show to the contrary. If they have made any argument at all, it is against the character of the railway and the route. That is an argument which might have been used, and which may be used, by the shareholders of the Grand Trunk when they come to consider the question whether they will confirm and approve the agreement entered into with the government. Hon. gentlemen opposite have not even brought into issue the discussion of the benefits which are to accrue to Canada if this project is hrouaht to a successful completion. They have attempted in small ways to say the route is not the proper one. But bear in mind that that is a question that is to be determined by the engineers and by the government later on. The best route is to be followed, and the best course is to be taken, in attaining the object it is desired to attain. There was another feature. It had been heralded abroad that the government is doing an improvident thing in building the road from Winnipeg to Moncton and handing it over to the Grand Trunk Pacific under lease for fifty years. Hon. gentlemen opposite attempt'to excite the prejudices of the people by saying that the government is building this road and giving it to a company for a period of time. Now, they fail to tell the country that for the whole cost of that road no burdens will be placed upon the people, because the company will repay every dollar of interest after a certain period of time. And yet, while this impression is being-not made, but attempted to be made by hon. gentlemen opposite, my hon. friend from South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) last night made a most remarkable statement. He said, speaking of that portion of the contract providing for the construction of the road between Winnipeg and Moncton, that the company would be glad to get rid of this section of the great transcontinental line.
Now, if this is a great boon to the company, and if we are asked to deplore
the fact that the Grand Trunk Pacific is given a lease and management of the road for fifty years, surely the boon is to the company, else why the complaint ? Yet the hon. member for South Lanark says that the company will be glad to get rid of the obligation of running that road, will be glad to get free from that portion of the agreement. Surely these two positions are entirely inconsistent, surely hon. gentlemen are wrong in the one contention or in the other. It seems to me they are wrong when they claim that we ought not to give these powers to the Grand Trunk Pacific, because the Grand Trunk Pacific has entered into this agreement, and 1 feel sure that when men of the business skill, men having all the qualifications to carry on a great enterprise like this, are willing to enter into this agreement, it is because they expect to carry it through. Certainly, it is an agreement for the benefit of Canada. Sir, if there is one thing for which I shall have reason to be thankful for hereafter when I look back over my life, it will be that I had some little share in contributing towards this great achievement. I believe it will be a great achievement without any parallel heretofore in the history of Canada. I believe that it is the crowning achievement of a great life. I believe that Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the First Minister, when he comes to look back over his life, a life that has already been fruitful of great good to Canada, will look upon this as the crowning achievement of the most successful career in the history of Canada.

In attempting to occupy the time of the House in continuing this debate, I am aware of the fact that at the present stage of it I am unable to add anything very new, very spicy or very attractive. The ground has been travelled over so often, and the subject has been criticised so thoroughly, that I cannot hope to say very much new upon it at the present time. I had the pleasure of listening to an hon. gentleman that might be regarded above all others as the one who would be likely to give us some information as to the wisdom of this scheme, and its importance. I listened to him for the purpose of finding out the strongest arguments that could be advanced in favour of it by one who is said to be destined to fill the position lately occupied by the late Minister of Railways and Canals. I congratulate the country and his party as well upon the acquisition to their ranks when he reaches that post. The hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) started out by saying that he was reluctant to speak unkindly of the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals, who had been in a measure his political godfather, who had brought him into public life, and to whom lie was largely indebted for whatever success he had achieved in political life. Yet I re-

gretted to notice that when the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) Intimated, as I think unfairly, that the exMinister of Railways and Canals might be in his place yet if he had been allowed the privilege of handling the contracts in connection with that road, he was cheered to the echo by my hon. friend from Westmoreland. I thought how unkind human nature is sometimes.
The hon. gentleman is incorrect in his statement.

Then my eyesight must have deceived me, for I certainly thought X saw him cheer most vigorously that statement of the hon. member for North Norfolk, as well as many other statements criticising the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals.
I do not want to be placed in any false position. The hon. gentleman, I am sure, will take my word when I say that I did not do so. If X had, I would readily acknowledge it, but I did not.

Certainly I accept the hon. member's statement, because I do not wish to do him any injustice. But I do think, even if I had not credited him with that exhibition, that I saw quite enough last night and to-day to justify the same conclusion in the adverse criticisms that he has indulged in against the man to whom above all others he is indebted for his position in public life to-day.
I think perhaps the indebtedness is mutual.

Well, I am glad to know it. He referred to the hon. member for South I.anark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) and said that his speech was characterized by a poverty of argument and a strength of assertion. Well, there is no doubt whatever, after listening to the variegated and kalei-descopic way in which he handled this subject, that it was at least very different from that of the hon. member for South Lanark. What I heard reminded me of one of my Celtic friends, who, I think, came from the place where the hon. member for Guys-borough (Mr. Eraser) came from. He was located on a small ten-acre farm in our part of the country, and some of his neighbours who had moved out west, induced him to move to Manitoba. He went up there and bought a 50-acre farm, and when he came back he was asked how he liked it. He said that he enjoyed it very much, that it was so big that he could just wander over it all day like a goose enjoying himself. And so the hon. member for Westmoreland wandered over the subject, like that farmer who enjoyed himself wandering over his new farm so different from the one he had here. But whether the hon. gentleman contributed to the literature of the subject or the strength of the arguments advanced

on that side, I will leave to the judgment of the country at large. He followed that up by saying that the total outlay to the country in connection with this scheme would not involve more than $13,000,000 or $14,000,000, and he referred to the statement made by the Minister of Finance as being absolutely correct. Now, it has always staggered my comprehension to understand how such a conclusion was reached, because every one admits that the government is bound to build the eastern section, and. according to the fairest calculations made with regard to the cost of that section, it ranges from $55,000,000 to $75,000,000. Hon. gentlemen opposite admit as well that the money must be borrowed by the government from some source, that it must be expended in the construction of that road, and then for them to say that we are going to incur an expenditure of only $13,000,000 or $14,000,000 on the whole undertaking from Moncton in the east to Port Simpson in the west, is something that I cannot understand. I want one of these hon. gentlemen to go up to the. province of Ontario, appeal to one of the Ontario farmers and try to convince him with that kind of reasoning. I am inclined to think that the farmer would answer this way :	I do not understand
your reasoning. If I were to apply your reasoning to one of the ordinary operations of life upon the farm it would be something like this. I have a farm. I want to improve that farm, I borrow a couple of thousand dollars, I put up a magnificent building upon my farm, I put up good fences upon it, I make roads, and I provide the other conveniences of life, but to do that I have to put a mortgage against my farm for $2,000. The interest upon this $2,000 at three per cent, will only cost me $60 a year. Therefore, all these improvements have only cost me practically $60. Now, he would say that if your reasoning is correct I do not owe anything on the mortgage, the mortgage will be paid by somebody, I do not know when or how, but I do not even concern myself about it, because if I take the intelligent reasoning of the hon. Minister of Finance I do not owe the amount of that mortgage, I only owe $60 a year. I have paid that, X have paid everything and in fact I have only incurred an expenditure of $60 to accomplish all that I have done. That argument would be just as reasonable and just as logical as the argument presented to this House, that this new railway scheme is to be accomplished and that we will only incur an expenditure of $13,000,000 or $14,000,000 and that that is all the country is committed to. That argument is not logical and will not hold water. The hon. member for Westmoreland said that the policy of the government is a revolutionary action in connection with this scheme. I agree with him that it is a revolutionary action. We have nothing to equal it. It is

something new. It at least lias the merit of novelty. Then the hon. gentleman went on to struggle with the question of whether the railway can be built through central New Brunswick and be referred to some engineer's report which he did not quote, who the engineer was he did not tell us, when -the survey was made is unknown to the House, as far as anything he told us was concerned ; yet he observed that it was a better route than could be found in any part of New Brunswick and that if the road were built by that route it would be a valuable one for trade. Throughout the whole of the hon. gentleman's argument I noted one thing. He came back again and a <.-a i n to the hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) and he said some very unkind things as to that hon. gentleman decrying his province stating that he had said that his province is a poor province, that the land in the centre of it is n >
good, that it contains mountains and valleys over which railways could not be run, but I noticed throughout his whole argument that the gray spectre which confronted him, the nightmare which was troubling his dreams was what the hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals said 'in his argument in criticism of the Bill. He referred to that hon. gentleman seven times, but as soon as he took hold of the subject he dropped it as though it were a piece of hot iron. The thought that was passing through my mind was that he hesitated to proceed because of tlie consciousness of the ingratitude he displayed towards the hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals or because he knew that there would be a day of retribution in the future. But, he came back to the subject again and again; it was like Banquo's ghost that would not down. He made seven attempts to down it but he did not succeed, and when he tackled it for the seventh time he was as unsuccessful in rebutting the arguments of the hon. ex-minister as he was upon the first attempt. He gave this House no argument whatever to refute the strong and logical statements made by the hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals that this project was a most unwise one and that it was one which was altogether uncalled for. I have said that the hon. member for Westmoreland went back seven times to deal with the hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals. He tackled the hon. member-for South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) five times and he was quite as unfortunate in rebutting his arguments as in meeting those of the hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals. Then he travelled over New Brunswick six times. He went on to tell us about the wealth of central New Brunswick, of northern New Brunswick, of southern New Brunswick, and of the Tobique valley, rich in mines, in clay, in forest and fisheries, but he never told us how a railway could be built across it by any except the one line which he advocated. Then he came back to northern Quebec and travelled over the country four times, and then he went from Levis down to Edmundston. He told us about the Laurentian range, about its geological formation on one side, about its flora, and how rich its trees were, and he told us that the other side of the Laurentian range was exactly the same. Then he led us away up to Lake St. John and told us about that beautiful sheet of water and went over the rich agricultural prospects of that region. Then, he said that all the other sheets of water were equally good for agricultural purposes west and north of that. I thought lie was going to supplant the Minister of Agriculture. Then, he brought us back again, travelled up the mountain and travelled down again and finally came to the question of the government ownership of railways. His speech reminded me of a trip that I took last fall to Rossland. Travelling over the Canadian Pacific Railway you leave Robson and you discover that the engineers have adopted a peculiar way of getting up these mountains. They had to overcome a rise of several hundred feet so they built the road up a little then back again and up a litle higher, then back again, and then a little higher still. You are carried upwards for a time and then you are carried back again.
Just like Jack and Jill.

Yes, something like Jack and Jill. You are carried back again on what is called the switch-back and each time you rise a little higher and the engine is puffing and panting and toiling ever on and up until it rises to the top of the mountain just like the hon. member for Westmoreland. He went back and forth seven or eight times until he led us up to the top of the mountain and when he looked down from it along the road there was nothing but hills upon hills, desolation and the remains of trees that had burned, under growth and vegetation which had come up afterwards. He said that there were rich mines below but we had not unearthed them yet, and he spoke of the unlimited wealth that we were likely to bring to light somewhere but he did not tell us where it was or when it was to occur, and in this performance I think he displayed a strong resemblance to the locomotive carrying us to the mountain top. He did not present one argument in favour of the contention which he was advancing and he left it a't last in despair. Then, last night he occupied the floor for forty-five minutes. He first gave us a very nice introduction and then he proceeded with a reading of thirty minutes duration. The reading was not very attractive, I suppose, because the light was bad. but after forty-five minutes he collapsed for want of breath or argument. I do not know which. He tackled it again this morning and he gave us another exhibition of his reading qualities and this was better because the light was better, but

he finally abandoned that and dealt with some other questions in a manner which he was pleased to represent to the House as argument.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Emmerson) announced that there would be no difficulty whatever in building a railway through New Brunswick, but he could not exactly say where this railway was going. However lie thought it would reach St. John ultimately, indicating that St. John was the most important point for that railway to reach. \\ hen he spoke before in the House, he told us that the new railway would shorten the distance by 1200 miles, which was a much more generous estimate than that ventured by the Minister of Finance or others on that side, but to-day the member for Westmoreland did not risk saying how much the distance would be shortened. The hon. gentleman admitted that government ownership of railways was a failure and that the experience in European countries would show this, but at all events he was certain that any work done by the government would cost more than if done by private individuals. I could not help picturing the contrast between this language and the language he used in the Railway Committee, when he was strongly advocating the extension of the Intercolonial Railway to the Georgian bay with the object of ultimately continuing it to the west. Then he was defending the scheme of the ex-Minister of Railways for all he was worth, but now that hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Blair) and he are not In accord. I wonder whether the portfolio of Railways looming up in the distance had anything to do with so suddenly changing his logic and his arguments. The hon. member (Mr. Emmerson) also reminded us that he was painfully making history in his two-hours speech.' Well, we all know that he was doing something painfully, and if it was history he was making. I can tell him that it will never be read to the credit of himself or the party he supports in this project. It is history he will regret, and when generations yet unborn come to read it, they will treat it as a record of folly on the part of this government.
Do you mean to say that any one yet unborn would read that speech ?

Possibly they may read it out of curiosity. Perhaps the hon. gentleman (Mr. Emmerson) was excusable if he had the idea that he was making history, but he certainly was grinding out history at a fearful cost to the finances of the country and the feelings of the people who listened to him.
The hon. Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Sil'ton) presented the strongest argument from the government benches in defence of this extraordinary scheme, and I wish to refer for a moment to what he did say. The most noticeable thing about his | Mr. SPROULE.
speech was the manner in which he dodged around knotty points. Here is an example which will serve as a fair illustration of his procedure. To strengthen his contention that it was desirable to have another all-rail route to the west, he quoted me as saying that if the lmssibilities and probabilities of that great west were realized, we might expect that there would be 400,000,000 bushels of grain to handle, and that to carry this it would take not one railway or two railways, but a dozen railways. He tried to justify himself from this statement, in his proposal to build another railway. I drew the minister's attention to the fact that this argument was very unfair to the member for East Grey, and that it had no foundation in fact. The truth is that what I did say was, that if the hopes of the people of the west were realized, as to the rapid influx of population to the west and the expansion of agricultural life, they would in time raise 400,000,000 bushels of grain, and if they required to have that immense quantity hauled within the two or three months between the commencement of the harvest and the closing of navigation, twelve railroads would not be able to .accomplish the task within that short period. I pointed out that it would be impossible to handle such a production of grain in the short time within which they are anxious to rush it out, and I went on to say that even suppose a dozen railways could do it, it would not be the part of wisdom for them to try to do it, because it would be unprofitable, Inasmuch as during the balance of the year these railways would be lying idle. That is a fair sample of the mode of argument which the Minister of the Interior pursued. He reminded me of the Artful Dodger in one of Dickens' novels. We know that the Artful Dodger was an adept in dodging around here and there, and making people believe there was something happening that never did happen ; one time he was in your pocket and.another time out of it, and again he was under your arm or behind your back, but you never could know exactly where to place him. The minister gave us a great many quotations, but if they were all as fallacious as those which I personally know to be fallacious, then we can pin very lijttle faith in his statements. He treated 'the member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) just in the same way as he treated the member for East Grey. His arguments were notoriously weak and notoriously unfair as well. The hon. minister proceeded to tell us that when a railway company applied to parliament for a charter, they didn't have surveys and plans and specifications. That may be true, but when they are applying for an Act of parliament they are not commencing to build the road, and before they spend a single dollar in construction they will have their plans and their surveys and their estimates made as to what the road will cost, and nil this information will be submitted

to the board of directors beforehand. Have we not a- right to ask the government to give us that information which the engineer of any railway company would give to his directors, before they would deem it wise or unwise to embark in the scheme. But he gave that as a reason why the government were justified in taking up this scheme without the information we ought to have to enable us to judge of it wisely.
He says he is prepared, as a matter of government policy, to liberally subsidize railways, even colonization railways. Well, we want to know where he stands on that question, because, so far as I can judge, the sentiment of the great agricultural classes of my province at least is opposed to subsidizing railways liberally ; and the hon. gentleman is not in accord either with the sentiment of the farmers of his own province, if I may judge by what I see in the press, nor the sentiment of the farmers of the province of Ontario. When the government give us a policy of this gigantic character, they ought to give us the information we desire to have.
The hon. gentleman, dealing with the objection that we cannot successfully have running powders over the line from Winnipeg to Moncton, said that was effectually disposed of by the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton). How did he dispose of it ? He told us that the Canada Southern and the Grand Trunk were running over the same section of road for 220 miles in western Ontario. The hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) pointed out the other night that while through freight might be carried over a short line of railway, it could not bp carried equally well over a long line, because it would be necessary to change the [DOT]engines and provide a fuel and water supply, a double set of hands, round houses for the storage of engines, and many other things, that would not be required on a sli rt line. The hon. Minister of the Interior reminds us that it was claimed that the railway might take through freight, but it could not take local freight, and he said the hon. member for North Norfolk had disposed of that by saying that he himself had shipped local freight on the line I have referred to. Did the hon. member for North Norfolk say that it was a matter of common occurrence that the people of the country could use that railway for handling local freight ? The hon. member for Hamilton declares that they do not ; the hon. member for East Elgin (Mr. Ingram), who lives in the locality, declares that they do not. Therefore, there is no conclusive argument to show that it is possible for the Grand Trunk Pacific Company to give running powers over 1,800 miles of railway to other companies.
The hon. gentleman went on to say that the arguments addressed to the House by the hon. member for Hamilton were futile, nbsurd and ridiculous-why ? Because he
said that if you parallel the Intercolonial, you are going to injure its earning powers. In answer to that the hon. gentleman declared that the earning powers of a railway are generally increased by the construction of another railway through the same part of the country ; and as an evidence of that he stated that the property of the Grand Trunk Railway was never so valuable until after the Canadian Pacific Railway was built, and therefore he expects us to conclude that if the Intercolonial Railway from Montreal to Moncton is paralleled, its earning powers will not be impaired nor the value of the property reduced. Well, to say that is to say something that the experience of life does not bear out. We will suppose that there are 10,000 tons of freight from the west to be carried from L6vis to Moncton or St. John. If that is carried by one railway to-day and two railways carry it in the future, will the earnings of the two roads not be what were originally the earnings of one ? It is true, the freight will be somewhat increased ; but a portion of the freight of the first road is of necessity taken from it. If the development of the western country brought more freight to Quebec to be taken eastward, would it not be handled by the Intercolonial Railway, and would not the earnings of that railway be increased to that extent by this new7 road, if it is ever built, and if it is a success ?
The hon. gentleman refers to the statement that this policy is an abandonment of the government's policy in extending the Intercolonial Railway to Montreal, and he holds that it is not, because the Intercolonial was not brought to Montreal to enable it to get a portion of the grain traffic from the w7est, but for the purpose of reaching one of the great commercial centres for commercial purposes. We were told, over and over again, when we purchased the Drummond Counties Railway and brought the Intercolonial Railway to Montreal, that it wms for the purpose of increasing its earning powders by securing additional freight, so that instead of having deficits in the running of that railway, every year we wmuld have a surplus. Was not that the argument advanced by every hon. member on that side of the House ? I say it wms.
The hon. gentleman said that the first proposal of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, which was for a railway from North Bay to the west, was not a good scheme, and that he would not support it. Why wrould he not support it ? Because if that railway succeeded in bringing trade from the west, it was trade that was going to Portland. My answer is, could the government not just as well have made it a condition that the trade brought over that line should go over the Intercolonial in the future as to make the agreement we have to-day ? They could do it quite as easily and as effectually. That would make the Intercolonial a more valuable property to Canada and give

us an all-rail Canadian route. Tlie hon. gentleman said : 'We tie the profitable portion of the line-speaking of the western section -to the unprofitable part of it, and condemn the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway to take the bad with the good and operate the two together.' Well, I propose to deal with that point later. He further said : ' The building of another line of railway as a competitor does not injure the present railway. If the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway carries out its contract, it will cost us no more than what the hon. Minister of Finance has said. The Grand Trunk Railway is worth more to-day on account of the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway.'
And he went on to argue that the high standing of the Grand Trunk Railway was undoubtedly guaranty that it would be able to pay the interest on the bonds and on the cost of the eastern section. But if the Grand Trunk Railway is worth so much to-day, how is it that it has never been able to pay us back anything on the $15,000,000 we gave it in 1855 or 1857 ? Why is it that from that day to the present, it has never been able to pay the interest on that loan ? Away back in 1855 or 1857, we loaned the Grand Trunk Railway $15,142,000. The simple interest on that amounted, at confederation, to $10,457,000 of which not a dollar has ever been paid. What does the debt amount to today ? There is an accumulation of interest since confederation of $32,708,000, making a total interest of $43,165,000, and a total indebtedness of $58,308,000 due the 30th June, 1903.. If it cannot pay us a dollar on that debt, is it any more likely to pay us any interest upon the heavy expenditure we must incur to build that road from Winnipeg to Moncton ? Remembering what has happened in the past, it does not seem to me that the outlook for our getting anything from the Grand Trunk Railway in the future or the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway very promising. We often hear it said how munificent we have been in our gifts to the Canadian Pacific Railway. But, if we compare the two companies, we will find that we have done much less for the Canadian Pacific Railwhy than for the Grand Trunk Railway, and we have had some return from the Canadian Pacific Railway which we are never likely to have from the Grand Trunk Railway.
What has the Grand Trunk Railway received from the public ? It received first the original loan of $15,000,000 on which there is an accumulation of interest since amounting to $43,165,000, making a total due in principal and interest of $58,308,179. In addition to these sums, the Grand Trunk Railway and its amalgamation have received :

aid	 1,354,797

From Ontario, municipal aid	 $5,723,954
Province ot Quebec, municipal aid.. 293,774

The amount given to the Great Western in 1869, when debt was compounded, was $1,152,568, and to the Northern Railway, in 1877, owned and run by the Grand Trunk Railway, $3,258,760. Or in other words, we have given to the Grand Trunk Railway up to date $75,614,208, of which we have never received a dollar in return, either principal or interest. Yet we are told that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway will surely pay the immense obligation it is undertaking, that Canada will be recouped every dollar, that Canada need not be afraid of the expense, because we have the Grand Trunk Railway behind the scheme. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, says the Minister of Finance, may be men of straw, but we have the Grand Trunk Railway, with its assets of $150,000,000, behind it. Therefore we can feel perfectly safe. We are in the hands of a company which will pay back every dollar to Canada. Well, I cannot say that I share this confidence.
I wish for a short time to direct my attention to what may be fairly regarded as the first and only policy ever initiated by the present government. It is a policy which is entirely its own, and by which it must either stand or fall. The wild, hilarious en-husiasm with which its advent was hailed was something seldom seen in this House. In its incoherency and unmeaningness it resembled the paroxysms of hysteria. One could not understand the enthusiasm, the joy, the acclaim with which that policy was hailed. The scene could only be likened to what is occasionally witnessed by a medical man in private families. He goes on a medical visit and has to remain a long time in the house. A number of women are present, a great interest is felt, and finally when the happy event is over, all is confusion and admiration and joy and sorrow all mixed up. What is the cause of it all ? It is because of the advent of a young heir. After ten or twelve years of married life, it is the first and only one. Unbounded is the general joy and great the general admiration, as the young hopeful is dangled before an admiring world. See what a rising star of the east has appeared, and just think what it shall do when it grows to be a man. Think of its future possibilities. In like manner, hon. gentlemen opposite admired this bantling of the government, looked upon it and at each other, and cheered and wondered that ever so much was accomplished. I leave it to the dry-nurses to handle it for the next few years, and after that, I will pass it over to the tender mercies of the electors of Canada, and I am quite sure they will deal with it. But what does it mean to Canada, this political monstrosity that has been born into the world, and at whose birth there has

875S
been such clapping of hands, such admiration, and such joy, and such sorrow, that these emotions seem the result of hysteria ? Time alone can tell. But, in the first place, let me say that its advent was at the most inopportune time that it could possibly present itself
They always come unexpectedly.

There Is another strange resemblance that I had not noted. It comes at the time when we should naturally begin to think it could never come-at the tail end of a long session, after the House has been struggling for five months to get through its duties, and when we might reasonably have expected to end our arduous labours and be free, each of us, to look after his own business. But this proposition comes before us at the end of a long session, when there is no time to consider it, no time to deal with it. It is altogether too important a matter to be forced on us in this way. And yet, we are told, that we are to have morning sittings. The excitement of the closing of the session is started so that we may rush it through without proper consideration and without affording the people of the country time to size it up through the press, and to understand what it is they are being committed to. The next question I ask is whether there have been any demands from the people in any section of the country for another transcontinental railway? Have the boards of trade asked for it? I do not know of a single one, except that one resolution was said to have been passed by a few members of the Toronto board of trade, a resolution engineered by my hon. friend from West York (Mr. Campbell). What gatherings of farmers have asked for it? What province has been clamouring for this scheme? Was it demanded in the west ? I do not think so, for hon. gentlemen opposite have been unable to show us that there has been any such demand. Has Ontario called for it? No, for I say distinctly that the sentiment of Ontario is against the subsidizing of railways.
Hear, hear.

That is the sentiment of Ontario; I say that without any hesitation. Was it demanded by New Brunswick? Well, we did not hear anything of it until this Grand Trunk Pacific scheme was launched. Was it called for in Cape Breton ? My hon. friend (Mr. .Tolmston, Cape Breton), who speaks of it, had not a word to say about it before this scheme was broached. He was in favour of extending the Intercolonial to Georgian bay. But, as to this new scheme, he was as dumb as the proverbial clam in his own part of the country. Was it demanded by the labour organization? By no means.
The government party have engineered through a few resolutions by those bodies since the scheme was proposed, but nothing was heard of it from that quarter before. From what class, then, does the demand for this road come ? From one ciass only- the grafters and exploiters; the same ciass of men who engineered the Crow's Nest pass scheme, and who profited by it so well; the same class of men who are forever hanging about parliament and the party in power trying to get something out of the state for which they give no return. True, we have had the clamour from that class. I see in one of the newspapers that this scheme is headed by Senator Cox, which leads another newspaper to speak of this as the march of Coxey's army. In view of that, I thought that there was a peculiar appropriateness in the words of the Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Sif-ton), that we had come to the parting of the ways. It will be remembered that Coxey organized a great army of tramps and set it travelling through a part of the United States and scattering desolation in its path. These tramps had their last grand rally at a certain point, where Coxey addressed ills hearers. He said : We have come to the parting of the ways; we had better divide here; half the army had better follow the course of empire and go west,, and the other travel east where the wise men came from, or if they don't like that they can go to Halifax. I think that when this Coxey's army divides, a large part of it will go to Halifax, when the people size them up.
Now, in connection with this scheme, we have no mandate from the people to undertake the building of a transcontinental railway, and they add to the debt of the country for that purpose a sum not less than $125,000,000. No government in Canada before has attempted such a gigantic scheme without first gaining the consent of the people. We are told that we built the Intercolonial, and that we decided to; build it before surveys had been made. True, but we built that road carrying out an agreement of confederation. We commenced to build the Canadian Pacific Railway without a complete survey, bjit again we were carrying out an agreement of confederation. We bad undertaken these tasks in order to gain the advantages that would accrue to Canada from the union of the west with the east and from the union of the maritime provinces with the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. But we had the mandate of the people for these works. In this case, there is no such mandate. This, it is said, is an attempt to solve the important problem of transportation which has been engaging tile attention of the government at various times since they came info power. For seven years we have heard about the great problem of transportation and about what hon. gentlemen opposite were going to do

Let me tell the hon. gentleman that it took five months to get a carload of grain from my ranch to the lakes; it remained all the time in the hands of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Surely, there was need for additional facilities between that country and the lakes.

I desire to say a word in answer to the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Douglas), who told me not very long ago that he did not care whether the Grand Trunk Pacific was built or not, because he had all the railway accommodation he wanted.

I was going to inquire how they handled their products now. They had between sixty and seventy million bushels of grain last year. From the commencement of the season of transportation of that grain until the 1st of July, there were forty-four million bushels came eastward, and the balance of it was either sent west or was consumed in the country. It was handled by one railway then only partially equipped, and every bushel of wheat was taken out of the country by the 1st July this year. The balance of the wheat either remained in the country or has gone westward to China and Japan. Now, if with their .present facilities, which are acknowledged to be very imperfect and which are being improved every day, they handled the bumper crop which was raised in that country last year and they had it out of the country by the first of July, it does not seem to me, although, there may have been some local blockade, that there was such trouble in getting the grain out of the country. If it be true that the crop was handled by one road which had given a contract for 20,000 additional cars and which had only got a fraction of that number for their needs during the season when the grain was handled ; if it be true that it was handled by one road which had given a contract for twenty-five additional locomotives and which had only got three or four : if that one road, only partially equipped and in an imperfect condition successfully handled that crop, admitting that there may have been local blockades with which I shall deal later on, then, I say the urgent haste will not be so apparent for additional transportation facilities between the east and the west as hon. gentlemen say. We -are told that they will not have a greater crop this year than last year. In what position will the railway be this year ? The Canadian Pacific Railway will have a great many more cars to handle the produce of the west, it will have a great many more engines, it will be better equipped for the work. The Canadian Northern has got into the country in the meantime and it is also tolerably well equipped to handle the produce. If one railway got the grain out by the first of July this year-the first one better equipped than it was last year, and the second one tolerably well equipped-will there be any great difficulty in them handling the same amount of grain this year-because it is not contended that there will be any more grain this year than last ? That does not justify the contention that there is an immediate and urgent need for further transportation facilities for the purpose of handling that grain. Let us inquire how that grain is handled ? First it is sent to the elevators in the country. There was elevator capacity for twenty-five million bushels last fall. They have 13,500,000 bushels of elevator capacity at Port Arthur and Fort William or they will have this fall. There are addi-

tional elevators being erected in the west this year, we are told, that will store 10,500,000 bushels of wheat at least. 'In addition to that at different ports on the Georgian bay there is elevator capacity for about 5,000,000 bushels of grain. What does that make in the aggregate ? It makes an aggregate of 54,000,000 bushels of grain, or 10,000,000 bushels more than were sent out of the country last year and they do not expect to have a larger crop this year than they had last. What will be the ordinary course in the handling of that grain V It will go first into the country elevators. The railway will be moving it eastward to the great inland port of Fort William and Port Arthur. Vessels will be carrying it to ports on the Georgian bay and south of the Georgian bay. As fast as the train can carry it from the west it will be landed at Port Arthur and Fort William, the elevators will run it out to the vessels and they will take it to the Georgian bay and the ports south of the Georgian bay and these elevators will be gradually filled up. This grain is moved eastward all the time and by the time the grain is threshed in the latter part of the season and by the time navigation closes about the middle of December a large portion of the grain will have gone eastward. Perhaps eight or ten million bushels will have been carried eastward and forty or fifty million bushels will be in the elevators of the west, in the elevators of Port Arthur and Fort William, and in the elevators on Georgian bay, and during the winter that grain will be distributed.. With these facilities for handling the grain, what do we require ? We require more elevator capacity in the west, at the lake ports on Lake Superior and on the Georgian bay. We can always get vessels enough to handle the grain after it reaches Port Arthur or Fort William, and the grain will be moved eastward all the time. We require proper facilities for bringing that grain from the elevators in the west to Port Arthur and Fort William. We are getting improved facilities every day. It is easy to provide them for the future without the expensive outlay which is involved in this scheme. That is the way the grain will be handled in the near future. How will it be handled in the distant future ? The grain produced in the eastern section of the prairie country will be sent eastward on the lines I have indicated. The elevators will have it stored ; from those elevators it will be taken to the lake ports, and it will be carried eastward all the time. But we will have a very valuable and increasing trade westward with China and Japan. A. magnificent trade is being rapidly built up with these countries and we will send millions of bushels of grain and barrels of flour to feed those 450 millions of people in that great eastern country who must depend in future on what we will be able to send them for a large portion of their food supply. Then, we will have an-

other route in the future. Where will the grain go from the Peace river district, the Edmonton district, the Prince Albert district, and away north and westward ? Iu the future that grain will be sent out by way of Hudson's Bay route. I have no doubt whatever of it. That is our great inland port. Just as sure as we are standing in this House to-day-I have said it before after carefuly analysing the conditions of that western country and the conclusion is more firmly fixed in my mind today-this will be one of the great routes of the future. Then, we will still have an increased amount of grain going eastward for two purposes-for the purpose of supplying food to the eastern provinces and even to the province of Ontario and for the purpose of transportation out of the country. We will have these routes in the future handling all the products of that great western country; China and Japan will be one route, the Hudson bay will be another route and the route by way of Port Arthur and Fort William will be the third. When you divide the amount of grain to be shipped out between these three routes there will not be the congestion that a great many people fear even if the development of that country in the future should be as great as most of us anticipate. Then, I say, we cannot and will not be able to utilize this scheme to carry grain from the Peace river country away through to Moncton, to transport it to St. John and load it on vessels to take it to Europe. It is an impracticable scheme. It never will be carried out in so far as carrying grain is concerned because no railway in the world can carry grain for 2,800 or 3,000 miles, and we have no example, as far as I know in the history of the world where grain has ever been carried for that distance on a railway. A large share of the grain will come east but there will be another disposition of that grain in the future which is not perhaps thought of much at the present time. The farmers in that country will change their system of farming.
They will do as they do in Ontario ; they will feed a large percentage of the grain they raise on their own farms, convert it into beef and pork, and send it out of the country in that profitable form. Half the wheat consumed in Ontario to-day is brought from Manitoba and the West. We raise more grain in Ontario than would feed our people if it were used for that purpose, but we have changed our system of farming, and we are feeding our grain to cattle, to hogs and to fowl, and we are conducting a profitable industry in that way. The people of the west will sometimes discover that the constant cropping of grain will impoverish their farms, and that they too will require to keep stock and feed that stock with a large proportion of the grain which they raise. If a proportion of the grain raised for export were stored in the elevators

at Port Arthur and the Georgian bay, there would be this great advantage, that during the winter season, when the railways were not otherwise amply employed, they could take carload after carload of that grain east. That system will also have the advantage of distributing the grain to the millers of Ontario, who are now using immense quantities of it. The manager of the institution at Peterborough told me the other day that in a short time when his factory would be running to its fullest capacity, they would be using from 10,000,000 to 15,000,000 bushels a year, in connection with the manufacture of cereal food. He told me that most of that grain would come from Manitoba and the West, and in addition to that they are going to build a large flour mill for the purpose of grinding flour in bond. The grain will be stored in their elevators on the Georgian bay, and as they require it, it will be brought to Peterborough by rail and ground into flour and shipped eastward. This is the means by which grain will come out of the West in the future. We have no reason to apprehend grain blockades. The fact is that taking all the possible conditions into consideration, even with the greater production in the West, we will not in the future have the difficulty in handling it that we experience to-day. 1 was for a short time engaged in the milling industry, and we found that for ten months out of the twelve our mills had to be supplied from the West. Notwithstanding that we are raising more grain in Ontario now than in times past, nearly half of the grain ground in our mills comes from the West. But it comes from the elevators on the Georgian bay. We bring it in the summer from Port Arthur to these elevators, and then it is distributed to the mills in Ontario. JvTot only do we use it for grinding into flour, but we use it for feeding our stock. It is also a fact that we get an immense quantity of bran and shorts from the West, because the supply of feed for our stock in the great province of Ontario requires that we should do so. We have no reason to fear that the grain of the West will not have sufficient facilities to find its way to market.
We are told, as another reason for the building of this railway, that it will afford a short route to the seaboard, and that it can carry traffic at the cheapest possible rates. According to the Finance Minister, this railway will be 2,800 miles in length to the foot of the Rockies. What railway can carry grain for 2,800 miles and make it pay ? There is no railway in the world that can do it. Neither can grain be carried at a profit from the more easterly points of Regina, Moosejaw or Prince Albert. Grain is being carried to-day from Winnipeg to Montreal for 11 cents a bushel, or it will be on the first of September. Why, if that railway were built to-morx-ow it could not carry grain at 11 cents a bushel for 1,400
miles. We may, therefore, dismiss that as a reason why this railway should be built at the present time, because there is no doubt that this railway cannot carry it as cheaply as it is being carried to-day by part water and part rail route. As another reason for the construction of this railway we were told that we should have a railway to an ocean port on all-Canadian territory, so that we would be independent of the Americans and the bonding privilege. Well, we can accomplish all that by building a line from Riviere du Loup to Edmundston, and thence to Moncton, a distance of 209 miles. We have the Canadian Pacific Railway, which is an all rail route through Canada, except where it crosses the state of Maine for a short distance. We have the Grand Trunk Railway going westward, and we have the Intercolonial Railway going eastward, and if we filled in that link from Rivi6re du Loup to Edmundston and thence to Moncton, we would have an all rail Canadian route, and we would be as independent of the Americans as this new railway can make us. That reason will not appeal to the Canadian people as a justification for the government undertaking this enormous expenditure. We are also told that the influx of immigration to the West makes it necessary that we should provide railway facilities for the future. Well, they are building new railways in the. West every day. The Grand Trunk Railway proposed to get into the Western territory if the government never adopted this scheme at all. They have their road now to North Bay, and their first proposal was to go through to the West. They would have done that whether the government interfered or not. Again we are told in support of this project that it will open up new territories for settlement in New Brunswick, Quebec and Ontario. We have had settlement going Into these new parts of the country for many years and has any one pretended that the existing lines are over taxed in supplying the needs of the settlers. We have a railway running from Calgary to Edmonton for ten years, and until within the last two years I am told that it never paid a cent upon the investment, and that it is only paying two per cent to-day. Has the settlement in that part of the country overtaxed the capacity of that railway ? Not at all. There is comparatively little settlement along that 198 miles of railway. I passed over it last fall, and the settlement was verv sparse. It has never been a paying road. Then, what has become of the Regina and Long Lake Railway, which has been built ten or twelve years ? Has the settlement along the line of that railway overtaxed its capacity ? It has nevei yet paid anything on the money invested in it. The' portions of that country through which these railways run are not half settled to-day. You might put hundreds of 1 thousands 'of people, without overcrowding

them, in the districts where we have transportation facilities already without overtaxing the capacity of the railways. I say that the supply of railways in many portions of the western country is ample, whereas, in other sections railway accommodation is badly needed. The Canadian Northern and the Canadian Pacific are building more railways every year.
Then we had that magnificent scheme for development of that country, devised and launched last year by the premier of Manitoba in his deal with the Northern Pacific and Canadian Northern, by which he secured to the country the advantage of 1,800 miles of railway-one of the most valuable deals, in my judgment, ever carried out in this country. Did he saddle the country with an expense of $125,000,000 to do it? Not a dollar. We are told that we must incur that expense to have control over the freight rates of this proposed line; but the premier of Manitoba secured control over the freight rates of those railways for ever without adding another dollar to the debt of Canada. We are told that we require to provide railway facilities for Manitoba and the North-west; but he secured those railway facilities and reduced the cost of transporting grain out of the country without incurring a dollar of expense. I am glad the bon. premier of Manitoba is here to grace this floor with his presence to-day. I say lie has done more for the west by that stroke of statesmanship a thousand times over than will ever be accomplished by this proposed scheme of the government.
I understand very well that our Northwest is a great country; I do not underestimate its value and importance. I know that the great future of Canada is bound up with the west, and I believe it will be necessary in the future to provide for a development that has been unparalleled in the history of this country. But we claim that tlxat can be done without the unwise expenditure or the heavy increase in the national debt involved in the scheme before us to-day. We know it can be and will be by other schemes less onerous and equally valuable, which will be initiated and carried out by the Conservative party in the future. What have we already done for that country ? We built the Canadian Pacific Railway. We are told that that great undertaking cost this country over $65,000,000 of cash and 25,000,000 acres of land. Was it an unwise expenditure, considering the condition of the country at the time? We were told last night what that country had cost us, and the value that had been given to it by the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway. I say that in proportion to what the Minister of the Interior says that great country is enhanced in value by that expenditure, in that proportion he justifies what the Conservative party has done in the past for the benefit of that Mr. SPROULE.
country. We have given assistance to the Grand Trunk Railway for the same purpose, and we are willing to give it assistance in the future, though we do not endorse this scheme, because we are as anxious and willing to provide for the future of that great country as the present government is. We have very lavishly subsidized the Canadian Northern, because we had control of the freight rates of that railway, and because we desired to increase the size of the spout that was carrying the grain out of the country. It would be an easy matter to double the tracks of the Canadian Northern and the Canadian Pacific, as I have no doubt it will be necessary to do in the near future, and in that way double their capacity for handling freight; and it could be done at very much less expense than this scheme will Involve. We have made very heavy expenditures upon our canals. We have been told by the gov-ernmtnt from year to year that they were perfecting our canal system to provide a means of transporting the grain from the west to the seaboard. Bast year they told us what wonderful things they had accomplished-they had finished the canals, which their predecessors had been dabbling with for years, and had provided a continuous water-course from Lake Superior to the St. Lawrence, through which the grain of the west would float along in palatial steamers to the ocean carriers, the bottle-nosed ships which were going to carry it to the markets of Europe. They claimed that they were developing every highway of commerce at once, unlike the Conservatives, who developed one and left the others, and that they had finally settled the great transportation problem. They had finished our canals, deepened our waterways, and provided more lights along the St. Lawrence. But now we are told that all this is futile, and that they have to devise another scheme. And the urgency of it is so great that they cannot wait even a few' months until the next session of parliament, but must introduce it at the end of the present session. What will this scheme involve to Canada if it is carried through? It will involve an addition to Canada's debt of at least $125,000,000. I have listened very carefully to the estimates made by every bon. gentleman who has spoken on the other side of the House, and I say that if you build such a road, having regard to its alignment and its gradients, which the hon. member for North Norfolk says must be equal to those of the New York Central, which bandies 2,000 tons in one train, I say that $125,000,000 will be added to the debt of Canada by the eastern section alone. I say that $125,000,000 will be added to the debt of Canada by the construction of that eastern section, and in saying that I am within the mark. I make the prophecy that provided we build the kind of railway declared to be neces-

sary for the carrying of grain in the future, we will add to the debt of Canada $125,000,000. No $13,000,000 will do' it. How do we stand to-day? We have spent up to the present on railways $258,800,000, and we have never grumbled at that expenditure, because it was for the development of the west and the east. On our canals we have spent $103,484,000, or on the two combined we have spent $362,345,000. We have at present, in round numbers, a national debt of $268,000,000, and by this project we will add to that debt at least $125,000,000. What will be our position then? We will owe about $400,000,000. I want the Canadian tax-bearer to understand what we are being committed to.
We will be bled white then.

Yes. This present year we have $9,733,000 of debt falling due, which must be provided for by another loan. Next year we will have $20,926,000 falling due, which must be provided for in like manner. In 1905 we shall have $4,866,000 falling due that must be taken up. In 1906 $12,166,000 will be due and will have to be met. So that up to the year 1900, when it is not claimed that this road will be finished, we shall have to provide for an amount falling due of $47,693,000, to meet which we will have to borrow money. In addition, we will have to provide $155,000,000 to carry out this undertaking. Add that to the debt we are carrying, and what will become of our credit ? Will we be able to borrow money at as low rate of interest as to-day ? I am very much afraid we will not. We are to-day on the wave of prosperity. Cycles of good and bad times follow each other as regularly as day and night, sunshine and cloud. And I am very much mistaken if the demoralization of stocks does not indicate that we are now on the verge of hard times. Let shrinkage of values continue, let there toe decrease in our importations and reduction in our revenue as the result, and where will we be ? Remember that we must raise inside of those six years very close on $200,000,000 by borrowing, and let me ask the hon. Minister of Finance what will then be the dilemma in which he will find himself, and how he will handle it ? My right hon. friend the First Minister smiles. Is it at something that is passing in his own head that he is smiling ?
It is what is passing through the head of my hon. friend that amuses me.

If the problem with which we are to be confronted amuses the right hon. gentleman, he is welcome to all the amusement he can derive from it. But careful, thoughtful business men will study out these things in their own mind, and will ask what solution the right hon. gentleman proposes, and he will be obliged to answer that inconvenient question. But it is said 275
that this heavy expenditure will tide us over the hard times. I admit that it will do some good, but it will be at an awful cost to the people, and whether the benefits we will receive from that heavy expenditure will make up for the additional burden of taxation caused by this heavy outlay, is something I am not prepared to even guess at.
I have said that the sentiment of the country, in Ontario at least, is against the subsidizing of railways largely in the future. Has the government had any mandate from the people to put through this project ? No. I challenge the Prime Minister to-day to dissolve this House and go to the country upon this scheme. Dare he risk it ? He dare not. If he should do it, and if the people should return him to power, then he may carry out his scheme and I shall not offer any objection. But when does he propose to appeal to the people ? Not until the die is cast. Not until it is too late for us to back out. Not before we are committed to one of the most gigantic follies ever proposed. We will not be able to get rid of this scheme by paying $328,000, as we did for our indiscreet railway venture into the Yukon. We will have to carry out the scheme in some way in the future and my sympathy will be, not for the right hon. gentleman, because I do not think he will be returned to office, but with the men who will be elected to office and on whom will fall the carrying out of this measure. Who wants this scheme ? The west do not want it. They do not consider it the best scheme. They do want more railways, but they say they do not want this railway. Does Ontario want it ? Wre have had no voice from Ontario calling for it. Who then wants it ? It is the Grand Trunk Railway and the grafters attached to that company, the men who have always been trying to exploit the country. But do the Grand Trunk want the eastern portion of the scheme ? We know they do not, for their proposition first was to build up from North Bay to the west. They very reluctantly allowed that eastern line to be tacked on tq the one that they proposed. My honest opinion is that they neither want it nor believe that it will be carried out. Why do I say so ? Because there is a very convenient clause in this Bill which I think was put in there for a specific purpose. The Grand Trunk want to get into the west and. under this arrangement, they will get into the west. But they do not want to go into the maritime provinces at all, and do not want to be obliged to build eastward of Montreal, nor do they want to build a new line from North Bay to Montreal. Section 21 of this Bill provides :
The Governor in Council shall have the power at any time to suspend the progress of the work on said eastern division until the then next session of parliament.
This is a very convenient section for a political scheme like this. The hope is that



this will carry the maritime provinces for the government, by holding out the hope of the expenditure upon another railway. 'It is hoped that it will carry Quebec on the same cry, and especially by the assistance of two or three millions that we are going to give to the Quebec bridge. In Ontario- why, no one knows what we are going to do in that northern country, building a railway through the great clay belt. The proposed expenditure in Ontario combined with the gerrymander, it is hoped, will carry that province. And, of course, the scheme will be in favour in the west. It is a political scheme, designed for the purpose of carrying elections and give the government another term of office. But I am inclined to think that, should they succeed, they will have their engineers report that this eastern section is an impracticable scheme, and so the government will submit the question to parliament. Don't you think you had better drop it ? In the meantime, the Grand Trunk will have its line in the west. It is to-be subsidized west from Winnipeg by the guarantee of bonds to the extent of $13,000 a mile on the prairie section and $30,000 a mile in the mountain section through to Port Simpson. With this they will have all they wanted, and they are hoping that the eastern section will be dropped. If all this results in giving the government another term of power, I do not think we shall hear much more about the eastern portion of the road. It is a purely political scheme. What advantage is it to the people of Canada to build a railway and then give it away ? We are told that the people of Canada will continue to own it. What advantage would it be to a farmer to build a house and barn on his farm, and then hand it over to another person for ten years without interest and for forty years after that at three per cent on the money ? I think the farmer would say : That is a bad investment forme ; better sell my farm and go into some other line. It is very well to say that the people of Canada will own this line. They tell a story of a little boy who was asked by a visitor, who owned a colt that was in the barnyard ? ' I do,' said the boy, 1 but father does as he likes with it.' This road would belong to the government, but the Grand Trunk would do as it liked with it. We own the road, but we give it away for fifty years, and, in my judgment, to" give a railroad away for fifty years is to give it away for ever. We are assured that we shall get the interest on the money. Well,
I have given you an account of what the Grand Trunk has done with us in the past. No man can say with certainty that they will pay that interest any more than they have paid the interest which they undertook to pay us years ago. We loaned them $15.000,000 to build the Grand Trunk Railway, i Have they paid three per cent on it ? Have they paid two per cent on it ? Have they paid even one per cent on it. They have not Mr. SPROULE.
paid a solitary dollar. We are told that their road is worth twice as much as it was before the Canadian Pacific Railway was built. Has this enabled them -to pay that interest ? Not a cent. And if this road is built and passed over to them, we shall receive no return, the interest will accumulate and will stand against -the country for the. time of the contract and for all time in future. A great deal is made of the argument that the right is retained in -the government under this contract to allow other companies to use this road on equal terms. Weil, we have heard enough argument on that subject to convince me, at all events at least, that this is utterly impracticable. Bet me add an instance to those already given. When we were chartering the Canadian Pacific Railway it was found necessary to establish a connecting link between it and the roads of western Ontario. So we built the Gravenhurst and Callender line, subsidizing it to the extent of $11,000 a mile so that it would be independent and all roads could have running powers over it. We surrounded it with every safeguard that able lawyers could devise, so as to assure the rights of all these railways. But it was thought necessary to give it into the possession of one road to handle, because we could not run it by a commission. What road should we give it to, was the question. There was -the Canadian Pacific Railway at one end and the Grand Trunk at the other. We decided to give it to the Grand Trunk, so as to have the greatest assurance of competition with the Canadian Pacific Railway. But, under -the conditions established, the Grand Trunk was to give full running rights to all other companies. The Grand Trunk entered into a contract with the Canadian Pacific Railway to use that road, and the Canadian Pacific Railway did use it for a few years. But has that arrangement been satisfactory ? Why, there was a dispute a few years ago when, for a whole summer the trade of Ontario was hampered and inconvenienced because of the failure of these two roads to agree. We had freight coming from the North-west to Toronto down toy way of Carleton Place, carried over two hundred miles of road more than was necessary merely on account of the disagreement between the roads. And this, notwithstanding that we had surrounded the independence of that link with every safeguard that the ablest lawyers in this House could suggest. This, is pretty good evidence that we are not likely to receive much benefit from retaining the nominal control over the proposed road that the hon. Minister of the Interior and his colleagues tell us that we shall retain. This idea of a number of roads using one line * in common is a delusion and a snare. If we could not, as in the case I have given, secure the independence of a road 198 miles long, how shall we secure the independence of a road 1,800 miles long ? There is not the slightest

[DOT]eliance of it in my opinion. But these are the arguments that are used to justify this proposal that the government shall build the expensive part of the road and then give it away for the benefit of the company-for, as I say, to lease this road for fifty years is practically to lease it for ever, and the interest will simply accumulate, as the interest has accumulated on the money we have already loaned the Grand Trunk. That money was loaned in 1845 and not a dollar of interest has been paid yet. Is there any guarantee that they will pay the interest upon this ? In my judgment there is not.
Then there is another thing. We have a juggling between three companies that seems to be inexplicable, unfathomable, and that we cannot properly analyze, an agreement between the Grand Trunk, the Grand Trunk Pacific and the National Railway belonging to the government. The government agree with the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the Grand Trunk Pacific has nothing behind it except the stocks they are going to subscribe. But the government tell us they have the full weight and power of the Grand Trunk behind them, and they say that the Grand Trunk Pacific may arrange to amalgamate with the Grand Trunk. We will have the government railway amalgamating with the Grand Trunk Pacific, and we will have the Grand Trunk Pacific amalgamating with the Grand Trunk. We will have two sets of stockholders, playing into the hands of the stockholders holding the stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and playing into the hands of the same stockholders that are holding the stock of the Grand Trunk, and they can manipulate it as they like, the contracts, the stocks, the bonds, the sales, or anything else, and no man in Canada to-day can say what will be the operations of these three companies combined in the future. No analysis of them can be made to-day, no intelligence in this House can explain, it to-day. I say, therefore, it is unwise, it is improvident and it is improper. Our past experience with the Grand Trunk justifies the belief that it would be unwise for us to undertake that scheme at the present time, and, therefore, I am opposed to it.
What does this scheme mean to the province I represent ? Suppose we build that road, and it is a success. -Suppose it carries all the grain from the west to the east, and the stuff from the east to the west, what does that mean to Ontario ? It means that in proportion as you make that road a great success, you impoverish the transportation routes we have to-day. You take away the trade that comes to-day to our Georgian bay ports in the east, that comes from Port Arthur and the head of Lake Superior in the west. It takes away the earning powers of the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Canada Atlantic Railway, the Grand Trunk Railway, and of the Ottawa and Parry Sound Railway. It reduces their 275j
earning powers to the same extent as you make this other line a success. You must, therefore, do it at their expense. You must do it at the expense of our harbours, at the expense of the towns and villages along the line of the Georgian bay, at the expense of Collingwood, of Midland, of Penetangui-shene, of Parry Sound, of Meaford, of Owen Sound, of Kincardine, of all those lake ports that are handling that trade to-day. You will do it at their expense, you will sidetrack all the populous towns and cities in western Ontario. You will take the grain trade of the country away from them, and leave us hundreds of miles off this great artery of commerce, if it turns out to be what its sanguine supporters claim it will be. We were told from the government benches the other night, that the road is going to carry cattle from Ontario to the west.
