Mr. Speaker, I must first of all apologize to you and to the House for attempting to speak in a language that is not my mother tongue, but I feel it my duty as a Canadian holding a mandate from the people, to express in as concise and clear a manner as X possibly can my opinions on this question of national importance. I shall not detain the House at any length, because I am well aware that already the arguments on this question, pro and con, have been fully adduced. It has been my privilege to sit in this House since 1896, and during this comparatively long parliamentary period no question has ever been brought before this parliament to compare in magnitude with the present proposal. Indeed, one must go back to the old days of 1878 and 1879, when the Canadian Pacific Railway contract was explained to the House by Sir Charles Tupper, then Minister of Railways and Canals, to find a parallel to the present situation. Sir Charles Tupper, in 1879, presented his famous motion by which the Canadian Pacific Railway contract was to become a government measure. It reads as follows
That engagements have been entered into with British Columbia as a condition of union with Canada ; that a line of railway to connect the Atlantic with the Pacific shall be constructed with all practical speed. That the Canadian Pacific Railway would form a great imperial highway across the continent of America entirely on British soil, and would provide a new and important route from England to Australia, to India and to all the dependencies of Great Britain in the Pacific ; as also to China and Japan.
That reports from the mother country set forth an unprecedented state of enforced idleness of the working classes, and the possibility of a scheme of relief on a large scale being found indispensable to alleviate destitution.
That the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway would afford immediate employment to numbers of workmen, and would open up vast tracts of fertile land for occupation, and thus would form a ready outlet for the overpopulated districts of Great Britain and other European countries.
And, Sir, again to-day,'notwithstanding what has been asserted by my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproulel, the countay demands that a new transcontinental railway shall be built with all practical speed, as 25 years ago it demanded the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway. A quarter of a century ago the announcement was made that a transcontinental railway should be built as an all-Canadian route, and to-day

Canada demands that this promise be implemented by the construction of a second national line, thereby giving employment to numbers of workingmen and opening up fertile lands to the tillers of the soil. It has been said Sir, that time is a great healer, and it may also be said that time is a great educator. Who amongst the old parliamentarians who sat in this House in 1878 and 1879, could have then ventured to predict that the day would come when the question of a new transcontinental' would become a live issue in Canadian politics ? Much as we may differ on details of this Bill, much as we may differ as to some of its features yet the necessity in which the government finds itstlf to present such a measure to the House and to the country at this juncture must indeed be regarded as a happy necessity. This policy is not a monument of folly, as was so inaptly said by the member for East Grey. It is a bold and it is an aggressive policy, but one which is sanctioned by the Canadian people. I fully recognize that bon. gentlemen on the other side would be remiss in their duty if they did not criticise the details of this measure as members of His Majesty's loyal opposition. Governments, after all, are only human; we all know the truth of the old Latin maxim, Tnunanum est errare'. The Oposition, under our parliamentary system, exists for the very purpose of preventing the adoption of any measure which may not be desired by the people, and one of its attributes is to criticise in every detail any proposal of the government which it may consider is unduly pressed before the House. It is the 'duty of an opposition to discredit the economy and show the weak points of such a measure. But in my judgment there are broad propositions in this enactment which should rally the unanimous support of the House, as they will rally the unanimous support of the country.
First, as to the necessity for providing new transportation facilities there is no question. We are all unanimous on that point. As to the imperative need of keeping Canadian trade within our own control instead of permitting it to flow year after year into American channels, there is no difference of opinion. As to freeing our country from commerical bondage, as to the expediency of opening up the ports of our Atlantic \ sea-boards, as to the wisdom of developing new Ontario, new Quebec, the prairies of the west, and the great lone land on the north of the Canadian Pacific Railway, we are all of one) mind. This policy of the government is a broad one, and its very essence makes for Canadian solidarity, Canadian unity, Canadian commercial independence* and Canadian stability.

not think it Is because I can compare my ability with his. The government has been charged with hasty action in this matter. We are told that public opinion is not ripe, and that this scheme has not yet been matured. Let me tell the hon. gentleman, as a French Canadian, that if there is one thing which early in my political life I came to recognize, it was the pluck, the

grasping power, the grit of the British people ; and this is a measure which in its very essence shows these British characteristics, because the government realize quickly and sharply that it was wanted by the country. Let me recall to the hon. gentleman a historical incident. On the 26th of November, 1876, late at night, one of the editors of the London ' Times ' called on Lord Beaconsfield, who was then the Prime Minister of England, and told him that he had learned during the day that the then Viceroy of Egypt, being in financial straits, was looking for a syndicate to purchase his shares in the Suez canal. At once Lord Beaconsfield, without consulting parliament, summoned the few colleagues he could gather together in the city of Loudon, and the result was that that very night he pledged the credit of Great Britain to a very large amount for the purchase of those shares. It was a bold stroke, and it was bitterly criticised by some members of the opposition ; but, Sir, the people of Great Britain knew what was pluck, what was energy, what was true statesmanship, and posterity will for ever declare that Lord Beaconsfield, a man of foreign extraction but of British citizenship, like our own premier, rendered a most valuable service to Great Britain for the part she has to play on the European continent.
My hon. friend this afternoon stated that there was no demand for this project, that public opinion had not pronounced upon it, except some railway grafters. On this financial basis the promoters of this enterprise would he prepared to suggest the following advantages to Canada, advantages Mr. LEMIEUX.
which have never yet been offered to the country by any other railway corporation :-
1.	To construct the entire road with steel rails and steel bridges of Canadian manufacture, thus offering to the new steel and iron works at Sydney, Midland, Sault Ste. Marie and Hamilton an immediate market for an immense quantity of steel.
2.	To give free transportation from Quebec to any point on its line for all immigrants and bona fide new settlers and their effects.
3.	To carry wheat from all points on its line in the province of Manitoba to the ocean steamer at Chicoutimi or Quebec for nine cents per bushel, thus saving the farmer of .Manitoba about seven cents per bushel on present freight rates to the seaboard.
But there is more than that. If the hon. gentleman says that this scheme is only promoted by grafters, what will he think of my hon. friend who represents the county of Colchester (Mr. Gourley) ? Last winter, that lion, gentleman came from the great city of Truro to the small city of Quebec to attend the meeting of the Board of Trade, and there delivered an eloquent speech in favour of this very scheme. As far back as 1884 the Quebec legislature adopted resolutions in favour of a similar policy. This new transcontinental line will develop the resources of new Quebec to an extent which I cannot describe. The right hon. the first minister was taunted by the leader of the Opposition and the Conservative press for having made an oratorical display in presenting this measure to the House. Weil, I have read very carefully the reports which have been published on the new district to be opened up by this railway and according to these reports the northern region of Quebec will benefit to an extent it is difficult to overestimate. If you will permit me, I shall read opinions given by people who were in a position to know, of the nature of the soil, of the minerals found and the other resources of these vast domains. In the great speech which he delivered, the Prime Minister spoke of the missionaries, the voya-geurs and the trappers, who, in the olden days, explored the vast prairies of the west. He spoke of La Verendrye, whose sons were the first to climb to the summit of the Rocky mountains. This, Mr. Speaker, was no oratorical display, but an unvarnished statement of plain facts. This was a lesson in history to the young generation, who, in days to come, will be travelling through those distant regions in railway cars, those regions where 200 years ago the only white people ever seen there were those pioneers- men of my race and blood, and of whom I am justly proud. If you wish to know what is the nature of the soil you have to refer to the accounts given by those very men who crossed those vast plains many years ago. Here in the city of Ottawa you have the university conducted by the Oblate Fathers. As my hon. friends from the west know, the missionaries of this order have been the pioneers in the west. I have read the reports given by them and describing the Pine river valley.

the Peace river valley and Hudson bay district, and all these reports tend to show that there is in that distant land quite a new country just as rich and fertile as the southern part of Manitoba and the North-west Territories. Amongst others I have read a report from Father Nedelec, an Oblate Father, and an Indian missionary, who answered several questions put to him by Mr. Scott, the secretary of the Trans-Canada Railway. Father Nedelec says :
The tountry is generally habitable, except a few places, chiefly along the coast. Along the east coast the fishing is good. All kinds of grain, except wheat and buckwheat, also fruit and vegetables, are, as a rule, grown with success, except a few scattered places along the coast. I find it difficult to say what population might be supported in this territory. There is room for millions with improved agriculture and the development of industries. In some places the climate is better than that of north of Germany, better than Norway, north of Scotland. Lake St. John, Newfoundland. In some parts the natural resources are magnificent, and others not so good. As a general rule it resembles Quebec and the district of Lake St. John. All I can say is that the country is larger and more habitable than can be imagined. The soil is generally of a clayey nature. Between Lake Temiscamingue and height of land, white and red pine, spruce, soft birch abound; on the other side of the height of land spruce, soft birch and cedar.
Another Oblate Father whom 1 know personally, who was one of my professors at the Ottawa University, gives similar evidence. I refer to Father Paradis, former missionary at Moose Factory. He says :
This territory is very suitable for settlement and the land is first-class. From Lake Temiscamingue which is 650 feet above the sea, the Moose factory, a distance of 300 miles is one black clay plain, very suitable for grain, and well wooded with maple and other hard woods. At the height of land, 920 feet above the sea. pine is found in abundance also some very large poplar. From Lake Abbittibbi to James bay the finest spruce in America is to be found, and on the south side of the mountain some red pine.
He then speaks of the temperature, after which he discusses the produce.
The best possible potatoes and all root crops are grown here. Grain has not been tested to any great extent. I think wheat would succeed as well as in Manitoba. Oats, hay and barley would certainly succeed. Natural hay, excellent for cattle raising, is very plentiful. Excellent beef is raised here.
Then he comes to minerals, and refers us to Dr. Bell's report. He said ;
See Dr. Bell's report. I find him very conscientious is his reports, gypsum abounds at. the mouth of the Abbittibbi river. I think there is coal and petroleum under the river. Iron is plentiful. Mineral springs abound.
I think this country might be compared to Germany in Europe and the Fort Albany district with Russia.
The climate resembles that of Kamouraska, with the same flowers, wild fruits, such as gooseberries, strawberries, juniper berries and cranberries.
Let me now refer to the report of Dr. Bell, head of the Geological Survey Department, on this same region ;
A considerable portion of the territory southward of James bay is fit for settlement. My own explorations have not extended eastward of the basin of Moose river. In that basin a great deal of good land is found between the watershed of the great lakes and the commencement of the low level country to the south-west of James bay. The soil is mostly brownish, gravelly loam and light coloured clay, with sand in some parts. In the coniferous forests, when the ground is level, the surface is apt to be covered with deep moss, but when this timber has been burnt off and replaced by deciduous trees the ground is dry. The summer and winter temperature resembles those of the county of Rimouski-the summers not so hot, nor the winter so cold as at Winnipeg. The average snow fall is about three feet or a little more, still not quite so great as about the city of Quebec. Potatoes and all kinds of root crops have been found to do remarkably well. Hay also grows luxuriantly. Barley would, I think, be a sure crop every year, and rye could also be grown with advantage.
I have had experiments made at New Brunswick House and at Norfolk bn the Abbittibbi river, with a great variety of field and garden seeds and the results proved that this region is capable of growing anything which can be raised, say in the county of Rimouski. I regard the region as well suited for stock raising and dairy farming and it is not1 unlikely to prove fit for grain also.
Minerals are to be found in this region ; nearly all the metals are to be looked for in the Huronian formation, a belt of which is believed to run all the way from near I ake Abbittibbi to the south of Lake Mistassini, and this would be crossed by any railway from Quebec to James bay. Iron and gypsum are abundant to the north-west of Moose Factory.
We have also the report of the Rev. Mr. Bompas, the Anglican Missionary at Hudson's bay. 1st. What proportion, approximately, of the territory in question, south of East Main river, and west of Lake Mistassini, would you consider to be fit for settlement ?
A. From what can be seen by following the principal watercourses and occasional runs inland, I may say that over two-thirds of the land area should be fit for cultivation, for there are no mountains of any great extent, and the land generally rises in easy swells from the lower levels of the river basin, and unless extensive swamps may exist in the level plains between the main waterways, there is no reason why the greater part of the country would not be fit for settlement, should climatic conditions prove favourable.
He speaks of the climate and then goes on to a description of the grain and other crops :
4th. What description of grain and root crops do you consider could be profitably raised

it there were railway communications through the centre of this territory ? And is the country suitable for raising live stock !
A. Oats, barley, pease and buckwheat. Wheat has been raised at Waswanipy, about the centre of the' region in question, and the grain grown from seed raised there succeeded as well as from the seed sent there by Dr. R. Bell, director of the Geological Survey, from the experimental farm.
5th. Is the country well timbered, and with what kind of timber ?
A. The country is, in general, well 'covered with spruce, the chief marketable timber ; poplar and bouleau (white birch) are also found in abundance, wherever forest fires have made their marks. The approach of your railway to Hudson's bay I think most valuable in every way, both in the way of commerce and in defence of the Dominion, if needful. Tour further course, by way of Norway House, Green lake, Athabasca Landing and Lesser Slave lake, I deem very advantageous in the way of commerce and partly for settlement of the country, and especially as a route of communication with the far north country of Mackenzie river and the far northern lakes, Great Slave lake and Great Bear lake, with their fine fur country and the rich timber and soil country of Athabasca.

In all the southern basin of this bay no mountains nor continuous highlands are to be met. Properly speaking, there are no basins, the river is simply running across vast plains level almost with the general surface of the soil.

Sir, I am familiar with the district through which it will pass, and I am only sorry to say that this road will not traverse the beautiful counties of Gaspe and Bona-venture. But I will not belittle this great question with local or selfish interests ; I will have an opportunity of speaking to the government, and of speaking loudly, when the time comes for the government to implement the promises that have been made by the previous Conservative administrations to the counties of Gaspe and Bona-venture many years ago. I say that the new1 line will not parallel the Intercolonial. There are points of divergence which range from 70 to 80 miles. As the leader of the government said the other day, there are mountains between those two lines. But what if the two lines were parallel ? We all remember that when the Canadian Pacific Railway was first constructed between Ottawa and Quebec at was contended that it would ruin the Richelieu Navigation Company, and also the Grand Trunk Railway Company, which runs south of the St. Law-ence. What has been the result ? The Richelieu and Ontario Navigation Company has never paid higher dividends than since the Canadian Pacific Railway was constructed. The Grand Trunk Company has doubled its traffic, and the part of the Canadian Pacific Railway line between Montreal and Ottawa and Quebec Is that part which pays the best. Moreover the Canadian Pacific Railway between Ottawa and Montreal has not only constructed a line on the north shore of the Ottawa river, but it has constructed the short line. We have added to the Intercolonial the Drummond County Railway, which was so vigorously oposed by our friends opposite, in order that more transportation facilities might be provided for the growing traffic of the Intercolonial Railway, and the Drummond Railway parallels the Grand Trunk.
Will this new line be a wheat carrying road ? Sir Wm. Van Horne and others have expressed grave doubts as to the probability of this road carrying any wheat east of Lake Superior. It has been said that an all-rail route could not compete with our water route as regards rates. I will admit that our water route will always give the harvests of the west a cheaper

transportation, provided we equip wisely and intelligently our harbours and channels, but no one can deny that we have a winter, and that during five or six months our river is closed. But this road will not only be a wheat carrying road. There will be in a near future an enormous traffic of the widest variety between the east and west. The wheat output must not only rivet our attention-far from it. Has there not sprung up a cattle trade ? Will not the western ranches increase year by year ? Who could deny that this cattle trade does not and shall not depend chiefly upon an all-rail route ? Besides, this new road through its connections in Ontario and Quebec, will afford our manufacturing interests an easier access to the western market.
I am not an extreme protectionist, but I can presume that some day or other our tariff may possibly be raised against the United States.
Why not at once ?
Time will tell.
But time will not wait.

Let me tell my hon. friend that when the tariff is raised, when we have duties as high as he desires, the whole country, Ontario and Quebec chiefly, according to his own statements, will be teeming with industries, and our manufacturing interests will be largely developed. Then, Sir, will my hon. friend be satisfied with the water route and will he not prefer to expedite his products and merchandise to his North-west consumers by the all-rail route ? But, I have been told that the allrail route can successfully compete with the water route. Of course, I may be wrong, I do not wish to prophesy upon such a doubtful subject, but I am told that immense quantities of wheat are sent from Chicago to New York by the all-rail route and that the proportion is even sixty per cent of the western wheat harvests ; that though the Chicago shippers have the option of the lake route in summer, the railways get their share of the traffic; that they hold their own and that they pay large dividends, although their lines are far from direct. What are the rates ? By the all-rail route from Chicago to New York the rate is 8-4 cents per bushel, the terminal charges are 1-25 cents a bushel, making the total rate 9455 cents per bushel. To-day the Canadian Pacific Railway charge for carriage on their rail and lake route from Winnipeg to Montreal, is 13-4 cents to 15'4 cents per bushel. Then, the American railways on an all-rail haul succeed in getting the rate nearly 4 cents below the Canadian Pacific Railway with its lake and rail route, and as I said a minute ago they pay 276
dividends. This is done by easy gradients as was explained the other night by the hon. member for North Norfolk. Therefore, if such is the case, we can safely hope that this new national transcontinental road may become a wheat carrying road.
Sir, the right hon. Prime Minister referred in his speech the other day to the possible hostile attitude of the United States. The hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals ridiculed the idea, and he added that during the seven years he had been in the cabinet he had not heard a thrill on this subject. Has he forgotten the attitude taken by the United States about our Yukon Territory ? Has he forgotten the attitude of the United States upon the Alaska boundary question ? I need not refer to our many baptisms of blood in former days not to speak of the filibustering raids before and since confederation, but can he forget the McKinley tariff and the Dingley tariff-which are an illustration of what a policy of discrimination can be towards a friendly neighbour ? Has he forgotten the Washington treaty of 1871, or how it was carried out by the United States ? Has he forgotten the draft treaty of 1874, a treaty which was prepared by the late Hon. George Brown, the father of the Liberal party in Ontario, a treaty signed by the British ambassador, by the Canadian representative and finally rejected by the United States Congress ? Has he forgotten the draft treaty of 1888 ? Has he forgotten their treatment of Canada in the Behring Sea award ? The right hon. Prime Minister said that a time may come when complications, which God forbid, might arise, which would bring about the cancellation of the bonding privilege. This statement was hailed with derisive cheers, and I was surprised to see with what levity, nay, with what scorn, such an announcement was received from hon. gentlemen opposite and from the Conservative press at large.
Sir, is it possible that in our day and generation, the hon. gentlemen should be, to that extent, at variance with themselves, and their principles ? I remember the day, not far distant, when our leaders were loudly accused of disloyalty because they advocated reciprocity with the United States. I remember those inflammatory speeches in which the Liberal party was roundly abused on account of its so-called annexationist proclivities. We were charged with disloyalty, nay worse, with treason. The echoes of the memorable campaign of 1891 still ring in my ears.
Times have changed, and the history of the last eight or ten years has proven how utterly false and despicable were those charges. But, Sir, where do the extreme loyalists of yore stand ? The idea of an all-Canadian route is despised ; a policy of ' Canada for the Canadians ' is received with contempt ! Yet, Sir,- is not the danger



pointed out by the Prime Minister a tangible one ? It may be argued that the bonding privilege is of mutual benefit to botli countries. Tliis I readily grant. But I make bold to say that the cancellation of the bonding privilege would injure Canada to a greater extent than the United States.
I can safely assert that not an insignificant portion of the American press and a very large body of aggressive American politicians-for reasons we can easily detect-are decidedly opposed to that bonding privilege. The New York ' Sun ' has been quoted, I could refer to the ' American Expansionist; ' the presidential message of Cleveland has been read, I could recall the deliberations of a special committee of the Congress appointed in 1890, to study the commercial relations with Canada. Has not the Canadian Pacific Railway itself been threatened many a time with the American hostility ? There are not a few who in the United States consider the Canadian Pacific Railway as a great military highway for the benefit of the imperial government.
Sir William Yan Horne took it upon himself to go to Boston and deliver a speech upon that very question. Speaking on December 12, 1892, he said :
It is pretty clear from the evidently inspired utterances of a section of the public press, and from the reported presence of a powerful lobby at Washington, that an organized attempt is to be made to secure legislation restricting or destroying the competition of the Canadian railway lines ; and in support of the movement the most absurd mis-statements are put out, calculated to excite prejudice against the Canadian railways. The Canadian Pacific Railway particularly is made to appear as an arm of the British empire sustained and kept alive by unlimited subsidies
for the purpose of destroying American commerce.
I have quoted this speech in order to demonstrate how uncertain and how frail is this bonding privilege. We are practically at the mercy of our powerful neighbour. Complications which I do not anticipate, but for which we may not be directly responsible, may at any time,, put an end to the bonding privilege. Such being the ease, apart from the purely commercial aspect, I say that the construction of a new transcontinental railway, binding together as it does those rich and vast territories and traversing Canadian soil from sea to sea, freeing us from any foreign bondage should any complications arise in the future, is a project of national importance to Canada.
Sir, can we afford to build a new transcontinental railway ? Canadian unity, Sir, has been accomplished by the patriotic, by the unfaltering work of three generations of men. The story of the marvellous change of which we are to-day the happy witnesses falls into three periods each with its own special watchword. The historic struggle for responsible government-for Canadian liberty, marks the first period. Then came confederation, bind-

ing together the several British provinces scattered over the North American continent. The third period bears witness to the long looked for unity of the Canadian nation, a unity brought about, not only by the obliteration of racial and religious prejudices through the social intercourse, but also-and in a large degree-through the civilizing influence of commercial relations, so highly

developed by this great agent of civilization -the railway.
Responsible government, confederation and Canadian unity, these are, Sir, the successive ideals which followed each other in a natural process of historic development. Before resuming my seat I can not help expressing the opinion that the launching of this second transcontinental railway will, in the eyes of history, be considered as the crowning act of the Prime Minister's parliamentary career. To him, as well as to his great rival, Sir John A. Macdonald, will be due the two great Canadian highways. Meternich's bitter phase in reference to Italy : It is but a geographical expression : shall never apply to Canada.'

I believe that Canada's further national development and welfare demands a second transcontinental railway. I believe that government ownership throughout of such a railway would be in the best interests of the country and people, both present and future. But as it has been shown that only one member of the cabinet, as it was, supported government ownership throughout, and as the feeling in parliament in its favour is confined to a few members on the Liberal side, to wait until belief in government ownership had grown sufficiently to ensure the building of a transcontinental railway as a government work, would mean leaving the western country without a competing outlet, either east or west, too long for the good of either west or east. If we cannot get what we want, the next best thing is to get what we can, on the best terms we can. That being the case, I support the present arrangement. Because it doubles the industrial and productive area of Canada. Because it doubles opportunity for every man in Canada. Because it offers the shortest and best all Canadian line from tide water to tide water, summer and winter. Because it is the only all-British railway across the continent under one management. Because it is so situated as to be most secure from foreign invasion ; giving depth, and therefore, strength to our country, to the advantage of both Canada and the empire. Because it gives development and competition in transportation to 1,200 miles of grain growing country in the west, as compared with 400 miles of such country developed by the Canadian Pacific Railway. Because it develops vast coal fields on the Saskatchewan, Athabasca, and Peace rivers, for the supply of fuel to the prairies. Because it gives the most northwesterly part of the prairie region, which is furthest from the Atlantic, a short outlet to the Pacific. Because it connects the railway system of Canada with 2,000 miles of steamboat navigation on the Athabasca, Peace. Liard and Mackenzie rivers, their great lakes, and the Arctic ocean. Because it develops mining and lumbering in, 2761
northern British Columbia and provides facilities for profitable interchange of mutual necessities between the prairies and mountain regions of the far west. Because it ensures a third railway outlet from and through the wheat fields to the lakes. Because it develops a thousand miles of northern Ontario and Quebec, at present unknown and inaccessible. Because it cuts nearly 200 miles off the present Intercolonial! distance between Quebec and Canada's nearest winter port, St. John. Because by government ownership and control of rates, with modern construction, and adequate equipment, it provides an all-year-round outlet for western grain ; and gives the merchants and manufacturers of eastern Canada profitable access to the market of the great west. Because it does this without land grant, tax exemption or provincial or local aid of any kind. Because it induces the investment of one hundred millions of British capital in Canada ; and correspondingly interests the British public in Canada's welfare. Because co-operation with the Grand Trunk Company secures effective, satisfactory and business-like operation ; ensures fulfilment of all engagements, provides business from the start, and secures the government from payment on its guarantee. Because by that cooperation all principal points in eastern Canada are put in direct connection with the west without extra cost. Because it transfers the through-traffic interests of the Grand Trunk, from the western states, to western Canada. Because it provides against over capitalization for effective government control of rates, and secures running rights to other roads throughout its whole length. Because an Atlantic outlet for the Canadian Northern, and extension of the Intercolonial to the wheat fields, is provided for without a cent of additional public cost. Because it gives maximum public control for a minimum public outlay, and absolute security for the financial responsibility assumed.
Mr. Speaker, as it is pretty late in the evening, aud as a number of our members have gone to their homes, I move the adjournment of the debate.

Mr. Speaker, though it is yet somewhat early in the evening, as I am sure my hon. friend has an important speech to make, and as the attendance in the House is rather slim, I feel inclined for my part to agree to the motion of my hon. friend. But I would like to intimate to the House-and in this I hope I shall have its support-that commencing on Monday next our sittings ought to be more extended in evening than they have been up to the present time this session. I think- and in so saying I believe I also express the feeling of the House-that it is time we * should think of such a thing as prorogation.

Therefore, I propose that on and after Monday next the House should sit late, and even pretty late.

I may say that the reason why a speaker on this side did not follow the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Lemieux) this evening was owing to an arrangement which we had that he would speak about one hour, and that the hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. Smith) would have an opportunity of beginning his speech not later than a quarter to ten; but as the hon. member for Gaspe spoke till about ten minutes past ten, the hon. member for Wentworth was precluded from making his speech this evening. I think this explanation is due to this side of the House.
I have no fault to find.

I wish to say, in answer to the Prime Minister, that I would like to listen, to the debate and understand it, and I can assure the right hon. gentleman, that sitting in the House from eleven o'clock in the morning till twelve at night, imposes upon any one, who cares to listen and understand, what is going on, a great mental task; and if he has anything to do beyond that time, he is driven from morning till night. Therefore, I would ask the Prime Minister, whether eleven or twelve o'clock, is not the latest hour, to which we shoull be called upon to sit ?
I do not know my hon. friend's feeling, but I may say that my mind is made up-I am ready to vote.

I assume that the right hon. gentleman has of course consulted the leader of the opposition, as I think he would be entitled to do, before he made this announcement. The right hon. gentleman knows that we have commenced two sessions per day; and, while we all devoutly hope for an early prorogation, at the same time, he knows that we have entered upon the consideration of a class of legislation that should occupy the greater part of an ordinary session, and I hope he will defer committing the House to an understanding that we are to sit very late. He must see that that has somewhat the appearance of forcing the measure through at a time when members are not in the same trim that they are earlier in the session.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) We are in splendid trim on this side of the House.
In a word, I wish to call the right hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that his announcement will not be very well received.

I have only to point out to my hon. friend, who is an old parliamentary hand, this fact, that this session we have not followed the rule which prevailed in my earlier days, when I first came into this parliament, not to adjourn

speechtext: before twelve o'clock, sometimes not till one o'clock. I do not intend to force the discussion. On the contrary, I think the opposition should have every latitude. But, on the other hand, my hon. friend must admit that we should not adjourn at half past ten, but should sit later.

The right hon. gentleman knows that if we have been adjourning early, it has been at the instance and for the convenience of his own supporters. I am not at all complaining of that, but I would like the right hon. gentleman, before he comes to a final conclusion, to consult the leader of the opposition. It is only fair, I think, that that should be done.

And at the time the right hon. gentleman first came to the House, the strenuous life was not as popular as it is now, and it depends on food and sleep. In those early days members of parliament had a stimulant of some kind, which enabled them to maintain an all night session, and which we do not have.

Motion agreed to, and debate adjourned.
